title: FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certification Prep
sub_title: Complete Prep for the FAA Remote Pilot Knowledge Test
description: Prepare to earn your FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate. Covers every knowledge-test area: Part 107 regulations, airspace and sectional charts, airport operations, weather, aircraft performance and loading, emergency procedures, aeronautical decision making, and radio communications.
text_content: This course prepares you for the FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Knowledge Test — the exam required to earn a Remote Pilot Certificate and fly small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) commercially. Units cover the Part 107 regulations, airspace classifications and charts, airport operations, weather, aircraft performance and loading, emergency procedures, aeronautical decision making, and radio communication procedures.

units.title: PART 107 REGULATIONS
units.sub_title: Rules for Civil Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS)
units.description: Apply the FAA's Part 107 rules governing commercial sUAS operations, covering pilot roles, operational limitations, airspace requirements, Remote ID compliance, waivers, and regulations for night flight and flight over people and moving objects.
units.text_content: Part 107 governs civil small unmanned aircraft (under 55 pounds) in the NAS. This unit covers applicability, crew roles, operating rules, waivers, Remote ID, operations over people and moving objects, and night operations.

sub_units.title: Applicability of Part 107
sub_units.description: Identify which small unmanned aircraft operations are governed by Part 107 and which operations are explicitly excluded.
sub_units.text_content:
The FAA published remote pilot certification and operating rules for civil small unmanned aircraft in August 2016. Part 107 oversees non-recreational and commercial operations of small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) in the National Airspace System (NAS).

Part 107 applies to any operation that directly or indirectly supports a business, nonprofit, government, or compensated purpose (monetary or non-monetary).

Drone operators no longer need special exemptions or permits from the FAA to fly—only a Remote Pilot certificate. Operators can fly without needing special exemptions, airworthiness requirements, pilot certification provisions, operating limitations, or external payload provisions. Initially, the rule did not permit sUAS operations at night or over people without a waiver.

Part 107 DOES NOT apply to: recreational/model aircraft operated in accordance with 49 U.S.C. 44809 (hobby and recreational use), public aircraft operations, amateur rockets, moored balloons, unmanned free balloons, kites, operations conducted outside the United States, air carrier operations, and operations conducted under Section 333 exemptions.

sub_units.title: Crew Roles and Responsibilities
sub_units.description: Understand the responsibilities, authority, communication, and coordination of each person involved in a Part 107 operation.
sub_units.text_content: A safe Part 107 operation depends on clear roles and effective communication. This section covers the Remote Pilot in Command, the person manipulating the flight controls, the visual observer, and broader flight crew coordination.

sub_units.title: Remote Pilot In Command (RPIC)
sub_units.description: Describe RPIC certification, authority, preflight duties, and emergency responsibilities under Part 107.
sub_units.text_content:
The person flying the drone must hold a Remote Pilot Certificate with a sUAS rating, or be under the direct supervision of someone who holds that certificate.

The RPIC has final authority and ultimate responsibility for the operation and safety of the sUAS and flight. The certificate must be easily accessible when flying.

The RPIC must be designated before or during the flight. The RPIC must ensure the sUA will pose no undue hazard to other people, aircraft, or property in the event of a loss of control, and must ensure the operation complies with all applicable regulations.

Preflight duties include conducting preflight checks of the aircraft and control system, verifying the aircraft is safe and airworthy, confirming registration requirements are met, ensuring Visual Line of Sight (VLOS) rules will be met, and briefing the crew (visual observer and person manipulating controls) on readiness and capability.

The RPIC has final authority to modify, delay, or cancel a flight. In a true in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the RPIC may deviate from Part 107 rules to the extent necessary to meet that emergency.

sub_units.title: Person Manipulating the Flight Controls
sub_units.description: Explain when a non-certificated person may manipulate flight controls and the supervision requirements for the RPIC.
sub_units.text_content:
Under Part 107, the person manipulating the flight controls is physically operating the drone's controls but is not necessarily the Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC).

If the person manipulating the flight controls is not a certificated remote pilot, they may operate the controls only if:
- The RPIC is supervising them directly.
- The RPIC has the ability to immediately take control, either by standing next to them or through a radio or override system.
- They understand the mission, safety procedures, and emergency actions.

sub_units.title: Visual Observer (VO)
sub_units.description: Explain the visual observer's role and when a VO is recommended to support situational awareness and VLOS.
sub_units.text_content: A Visual Observer (VO) assists the crew in avoiding hazards and obstacles and in maintaining situational awareness and VLOS. A VO is not always required but is recommended when mission complexity warrants extra eyes on the operation.

sub_units.title: Flight Crew Management and Communication
sub_units.description: Apply crew briefing, workload management, and communication methods including hands-free options and clock-position reporting.
sub_units.text_content:
Depending on operation complexity, additional crew may be needed beyond the RPIC, VO, and person manipulating the controls—for example payload operators, camera operators, or other specialists.

The RPIC is responsible for task distribution and workload management.

Pre-flight considerations include assessing weather, airspace, terrain, and obstacles; aircraft condition and airworthiness; and crew readiness (mental and physical).

Pre-flight communications must include a crew briefing on emergency procedures, contingency plans, and potential hazards. Preflight familiarization and inspection include reviewing manufacturer instructions, inspecting components (propellers, battery, control link), and ensuring required documentation is available.

Effective communication between crew members may use a two-way radio, cell phone, or other technology. The RPIC may choose any communication method as long as it is safe. If the person manipulating the flight controls cannot use a handheld device safely, use hands-free options such as an earpiece, headset, or speaker mode on a cell phone.

When flying, it is important for everyone to maintain situational awareness. Communicating the UA's location using clock coordinates is recommended: 12:00 straight ahead of the RPIC, 3:00 to the right, 6:00 behind, and 9:00 to the left.

If the UA goes out of VLOS for more than 15 seconds, initiate a failsafe return to home.

sub_units.title: Operating Rules
sub_units.description: Navigate the core Part 107 operating rules grouped in this section, from registration through speed, altitude, and visibility limits.
sub_units.text_content:
This unit follows the Part 107 regulations outline: applicability, crew roles, operational rules (registration through performance limits), waivers, Remote ID, operations over people and moving objects, and night operations.

Lessons in Operating Rules: registration and inspection; accident reporting; medical fitness; moving vehicles and property transport; general operation over people; VLOS; right-of-way; autonomous flight; preflight and airspace; operating limitations.

sub_units.title: Registration, Inspection, and Falsification
sub_units.description: Explain requirements for aircraft registration, mandatory compliance inspections, and penalties for falsifying records.
sub_units.text_content:
Aircraft Registration: All non-recreational drones must be registered according to 14 CFR Part 47 or Part 48. The registration number must be legibly displayed on the aircraft, and the RPIC must carry proof of registration physically or digitally.

Inspection, Testing, and Compliance: Upon request, the RPIC, person controlling the aircraft, or the owner must present a remote pilot certificate with a sUAS rating, photo ID with signature and date of birth, and any documents, records, or reports required under Part 107 to the FAA, NTSB, Federal, State, or local law enforcement, or TSA.

Upon request, the RPIC, visual observer, owner, operator, or person manipulating the controls must allow the FAA to inspect the aircraft and involved personnel, facilities, technical data, and any manufactured small UAS, and to witness any tests necessary to verify Part 107 compliance.

Falsification, Reproduction, or Alteration: Providing false information or fraudulently altering or reproducing required records or reports—including omissions—can result in denial, suspension, or revocation of a certificate or waiver, or civil penalties (fines).

sub_units.title: Accident Reporting, In-Flight Emergency, and Hazardous Operations
sub_units.description: Summarize rules for mandatory accident reporting, in-flight emergencies, and prohibitions against reckless or hazardous operations.
sub_units.text_content:
Accident Reporting: The RPIC must report an accident to the FAA within 10 days if it results in serious injury to any person or any loss of consciousness, or if it causes damage to property (other than the UAS) in excess of $500 to repair or replace (whichever is lower).

In-Flight Emergency: In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the RPIC may deviate from any rule in Part 107 to the extent necessary to meet that emergency. Upon request from the Administrator, the RPIC who deviates must send a written report.

Hazardous Operations: No person may operate a sUAS in a reckless manner that endangers the life or property of another—for example, continuing to fly in inclement weather or in an area with many buildings, trees, or other structures. No person may allow an object to be dropped from a sUAS in a manner that creates an undue hazard to persons or property.

sub_units.title: Medical Conditions, Alcohol, and Drugs
sub_units.description: Identify physical and mental fitness requirements for crew members, including prohibitions on operating while impaired by medical conditions, alcohol, or drugs.
sub_units.text_content:
Medical Condition: A medical certificate is not required to fly a sUAS or serve on the crew. However, if you know or have reason to believe your condition would interfere with safe operation, you must not fly. Examples include fatigue; medication that affects performance or situational awareness (including over-the-counter antihistamines and decongestants that may cause drowsiness); physical illness (flu, headaches) or mental illness; loss of hearing or voice that prevents communication; blurred vision that prevents satisfying see-and-avoid requirements; or temporary or permanent loss of the ability to control the drone effectively.

Alcohol or Drugs: No person controlling a sUAS or serving as a crew member may have a medical condition that could risk the safety of the operation (for example epilepsy), be under the influence of alcohol, use drugs that affect capabilities, have consumed alcohol within the previous 8 hours, or have an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. If requested by law enforcement, an individual must submit to a test to indicate alcohol concentration in the blood or breath.

sub_units.title: Operation Over People — General Rule
sub_units.description: State the baseline prohibition on flight over people and the three exceptions before applying category-specific requirements.
sub_units.text_content:
Except in certain category-based situations described later in this unit, no person may operate a sUA over a human being unless that person is:
- Directly participating in the operation of the sUA;
- Located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling sUA; or
- Otherwise covered by the approved category rules for operations over people (Categories 1–4).

This general rule applies before considering kinetic-energy categories, labeling, and sustained-flight restrictions over crowds or moving vehicles.

sub_units.title: Transportation of Property
sub_units.description: State when property may be transported under Part 107 and the interstate, District of Columbia, and territory restrictions that prohibit carriage for compensation.
sub_units.text_content: Transportation of Property: You may transport property under Part 107 if all operations are within one state, occur within a defined operating area, and remain fully compliant with all Part 107 requirements. You may not transport property under Part 107 if the operation is between places in the District of Columbia, crosses state lines, or in certain territories involves passing through international airspace (for example, some transport between Hawaiian islands).

sub_units.title: Operation From Moving Vehicles
sub_units.description: State the rules for operating a sUAS from a moving land or water vehicle, including the sparsely populated area requirement and the ban on flying from a moving aircraft.
sub_units.text_content: Operation From a Moving Vehicle: When in a moving land or water vehicle, no person may operate a sUA unless the sUA is flown over a sparsely populated area and the operation is not transporting another person's property for compensation or hire. You may not operate a sUA from a moving aircraft.

sub_units.title: Visual Line of Sight (VLOS) and Multi-Aircraft Rules
sub_units.description: Define Visual Line of Sight (VLOS) requirements, VO duties when a visual observer is used, and the prohibition on controlling more than one unmanned aircraft at a time.
sub_units.text_content:
Visual Line of Sight (VLOS): The RPIC, person manipulating the flight controls, and VO (if used) must be able to see the UA throughout the flight unaided (corrective lenses only) in order to know the aircraft's location; determine its attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; observe the airspace for other traffic or hazards; and determine that the UA does not endanger the life or property of another.

Throughout the entire flight, unaided vision (no binoculars) must be maintained by the RPIC and person manipulating the controls, or by a visual observer.

When a visual observer is used, the RPIC, the person manipulating the flight controls, and the VO must maintain effective communication with each other at all times, scan the airspace for any potential collision hazard, and maintain awareness of the position of the sUA through direct visual observation.

The VO must keep the unmanned aircraft in VLOS unaided (corrective lenses only). Briefly looking at the flight controller to locate the aircraft for a second or to check battery life—or when the aircraft is momentarily behind smoke or a chimney—is acceptable if VLOS is maintained overall.

Operation of Multiple Small Unmanned Aircraft: A person may not manipulate flight controls or act as RPIC or visual observer in the operation of more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time.

sub_units.title: Right-of-Way Rules and Operation Near Aircraft
sub_units.description: Explain the mandatory see-and-avoid requirement and the prohibition against interfering with manned aircraft operations.
sub_units.text_content:
All sUAS must yield the right of way to all aircraft (see and avoid). The sUAS must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear. No person may operate a sUA in a manner that creates a collision hazard.

To comply with see-and-avoid, the RPIC must fly the UA so that a manned aircraft pilot never needs to change flight path to avoid collision. The RPIC must know the UA's location and flight path at all times and remain aware of activity in the vicinity to avoid collision with people, property, or manned aircraft.

sub_units.title: Autonomous Flight and RPIC Responsibility
sub_units.description: Define autonomous flight under Part 107 and explain the RPIC's continued responsibility and ability to take control during programmed missions.
sub_units.text_content:
Autonomous flight means the drone can fly parts of its mission on its own using pre-programmed instructions—for example a set route or automatic return to home if signal is lost. Under Part 107, autonomous does not mean the drone is on its own: the RPIC remains fully responsible at all times.

When performing autonomous operations, the RPIC must have the ability to direct the sUA to ensure compliance with Part 107. If the control link is lost, the aircraft may continue a programmed mission or return to home. During autonomous flight, the RPIC must be able to command the aircraft to change route, altitude, or land—manually or through automation commands.

sub_units.title: Preflight Familiarization, Inspection, and Airspace Operations
sub_units.description: Outline preflight assessment requirements and restrictions on operating in controlled, prohibited, and restricted airspace.
sub_units.text_content:
Preflight Familiarization, Inspection, and Actions: Before flight, the RPIC must review the operating environment and assess hazards affecting persons or property on the surface or in the air, including local weather; local airspace and flight restrictions; location of persons and property on the surface; and other ground hazards.

The RPIC must ensure all persons directly participating are informed about operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards. The RPIC must ensure control links work, sufficient power exists for the intended flight, and any object attached or carried is secure and does not adversely affect flight characteristics or controllability. Before flight, the RPIC must verify the drone meets an approved category (1–4) when required and that documentation (certificate, registration, airworthiness certificate, waiver if needed) is available.

Operation in Certain Airspace: Operations in Class B, C, or D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport are prohibited unless prior authorization is obtained. A small drone must not interfere with manned aircraft traffic patterns or operations at any airport, heliport, or seaplane base—including causing manned aircraft to alter flight path or delay takeoff or landing. Operations in prohibited or restricted areas require authorization from the using or controlling agency. A NOTAM may establish a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) identifying the affected area and the hazard or condition.

sub_units.title: Operating Limitations
sub_units.description: State specific performance limitations for sUAS regarding speed, altitude, cloud clearance, and minimum visibility.
sub_units.text_content:
When operating a sUAS under Part 107:
- Groundspeed may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
- Altitude may not exceed 400 feet above ground level (AGL), unless the sUA is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure and does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
- Minimum flight visibility from the control station must be at least 3 statute miles (the average distance at which major unlit objects can be seen by day and major lighted objects by night).
- Minimum cloud clearance: at least 500 feet below the cloud and 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.

These restrictions may be waived if the operator demonstrates the operation can be conducted safely under a Certificate of Waiver.

sub_units.title: Waivers and Airspace Authorization
sub_units.description: Explain Certificate of Waiver requirements, which Part 107 rules may be waived, processing timelines, and how to obtain controlled-airspace authorization.
sub_units.text_content:
A waiver is special permission from the FAA that allows deviation from certain Part 107 rules only if the FAA believes the operation will still be safe. The FAA may issue a Certificate of Waiver (CoW) when you demonstrate the planned flight can be conducted safely.

Waiver Application Requirements: A request must contain a complete description of the proposed operation and a justification establishing that the operation can safely be conducted under the waiver terms. Explain how safety will be maintained using equipment, technology, and/or other strategies. Even if approved, the FAA may add conditions or limits. Failing to follow every condition and limitation makes the operation illegal.

Rules That May Be Waived: A CoW may be issued for operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft (no waiver will be issued to allow carriage of another person's property for compensation or hire by aircraft); visual observer requirements; visual line of sight aircraft operation (same compensation/hire limitation); daylight operations; anti-collision lights required for night and civil twilight; operation of multiple small unmanned aircraft; yielding the right of way; operation over people; operation in certain airspace; and operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft.

Application Process: Use the FAA waiver portal at https://aviationsafetyportal.faa.gov/. Submit at least 90 days before the proposed operation date. Requests submitted with less notice may not be processed in time and could be cancelled or denied. Your lateness may result in the inability to conduct proposed operations on your planned dates. Actual processing time varies depending on complexity and completeness of the application—complete the application as soon as you know your date. Airspace authorizations are generally processed faster than airspace waivers and on a first-come, first-served basis.

Emergencies: The FAA offers Special Governmental Interest (SGI) waivers for public safety, first responders, and critical organizations.

Airspace Authorization: Operations in controlled airspace require authorization. Part 107 remote pilots must use FAA DroneZone or a Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) provider. Do not contact ATC directly by radio or phone for drone authorization. ATC's primary role is keeping aircraft safe, supporting smooth traffic flow, and supporting national security and defense when needed.

sub_units.title: Remote ID Requirements
sub_units.description: Summarize the Remote ID rule timeline, registration scope, and the three compliance paths (Standard UA, broadcast module, FRIA).
sub_units.text_content:
In April 2021 the FAA introduced rules for Remote ID, operations over people and moving objects, and night operations under certain conditions. Remote ID became mandatory as of September 16, 2023 (except as stated in 14 CFR Part 89).

No person may operate a UA in the United States unless the operation meets Remote ID requirements. Remote ID is like a digital license plate broadcasting identity, location, altitude, and velocity so authorities and the public can see who is flying and whether the operation appears safe.

All drones require registration—including those flown for recreation, business, or public safety, including aircraft weighing less than 0.55 lbs.

There are three ways to meet identification requirements: Standard Remote ID UA, UA with a Remote ID broadcast module, or operation within an FAA-Recognized Identification Area (FRIA). The lessons below cover each path.

sub_units.title: Standard Remote ID
sub_units.description: Describe built-in Standard Remote ID requirements, broadcast content, and performance limits.
sub_units.text_content:
A Standard Remote ID unmanned aircraft is produced with built-in FAA Remote ID broadcast capability from takeoff to shutdown. New products must meet all Standard Remote ID requirements.

The drone serial number must match an FAA-accepted Declaration of Compliance and be linked to FAA registration before operation. The aircraft must self-test and must not take off if Remote ID is not functional. Remote ID must remain fully functional for the entire flight; land immediately if broadcasting fails.

Remote ID equipment must not be modified, blocked, or disabled. The aircraft must broadcast required information continuously over unlicensed radio frequency spectrum and be designed to maximize broadcast range. Standard Remote ID operations are limited to VLOS.

Remote ID is available to personal wireless devices in range using Bluetooth or Wi-Fi-type signals. The FAA and law enforcement may request access when needed.

Required broadcast elements include: Remote ID serial number; location and altitude; velocity; control station location and elevation; time mark; and emergency status.

sub_units.title: Remote ID Broadcast Module
sub_units.description: Explain retrofit broadcast modules, registration linkage, and broadcast content differences from Standard Remote ID.
sub_units.text_content:
A broadcast module is a device produced to meet FAA requirements that broadcasts identification and location information for the drone and takeoff location. It can be added to retrofit a drone with Remote ID capability.

The module serial number must be included in the UA registration. The UA or module must be fully functional from takeoff to shutdown, must self-test, and must not take off if Remote ID is not functional. Land immediately if broadcasting fails. The pilot must maintain VLOS throughout the flight when using a broadcast module.

From takeoff to shutdown the module broadcasts via radio frequency (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) with range comparable to Standard Remote ID: drone ID (serial number), location and altitude, velocity, takeoff location and elevation, and time mark.

sub_units.title: FRIA and Alternative Remote Identification
sub_units.description: Explain where Remote ID broadcast is not required, FRIA eligibility and renewal, and limited alternative compliance paths.
sub_units.text_content:
FAA-Recognized Identification Areas (FRIA) are geographic areas where drones may operate without broadcasting Remote ID. FRIAs are the only locations where routine operations may occur without broadcast. Both the drone and pilot must remain within the FRIA boundaries and within VLOS throughout the flight.

Only FAA-recognized Community Based Organizations (CBOs) and educational institutions (primary and secondary schools, trade schools, colleges, and universities) may request a FRIA. A FRIA is effective for 48 calendar months after FAA approval. Renewal requests must be submitted no later than 120 days before expiration. The FAA may terminate a FRIA if the application contained false information or if the area poses a risk to aviation, public safety, homeland security, or national security.

Alternative Remote Identification: The Administrator may authorize operations without Remote ID for aeronautical research or to demonstrate compliance with regulations. ADS-B Out equipment cannot be used to comply with Remote ID requirements. A foreign-registered drone with Remote ID may not be flown in the United States unless a Notice of Identification is submitted to the FAA.

sub_units.title: Flying Over People and Moving Objects
sub_units.description: Explain how the April 2021 rule change enables routine over-people and over-vehicle operations when category and documentation requirements are met.
sub_units.text_content:
On April 21, 2021, Part 107 was amended to permit operations over people, moving vehicles, and at night under certain conditions, eliminating the need for waivers for many typical operations.

Manufacturers demonstrate airworthiness for category operations through Means of Compliance (MoC) and Declaration of Compliance (DoC). Category-specific eligibility, sustained flight over crowds, and operations over moving vehicles are covered in the next section.

sub_units.title: Means of Compliance and Declaration of Compliance
sub_units.description: Distinguish MoC and DoC for operations over people and explain manufacturer and RPIC verification responsibilities.
sub_units.text_content:
Means of Compliance (MoC) is the FAA-approved method a manufacturer uses to show that a small unmanned aircraft meets safety requirements for operations over people under Part 107—including limits on exposed rotating parts, impact kinetic energy, and safety defects. There are three types: FAA-provided MoC, FAA-accepted or FAA-approved MoC submitted to the FAA, and custom MoC developed by applicants and approved if they demonstrate compliance.

Declaration of Compliance (DoC): The submitter must have proof the aircraft or broadcast module meets an FAA-accepted MoC; maintain a process to notify the public and FAA about unsafe conditions that make the aircraft non-compliant; allow FAA inspections, facility access, and records access; and confirm the aircraft has no safety defects. Records directly related to the DoC must be kept for two years (longer for custom MoC while the MoC remains accepted).

The RPIC is responsible for verifying category eligibility, labeling, and documentation before flight over people.

sub_units.title: Flying Over People: Category Operations
sub_units.description: Apply Category 1-4 eligibility requirements, sustained-flight restrictions over open-air assemblies, and rules for operations over moving vehicles.
sub_units.text_content: Category 1 through 4 eligibility, sustained flight over open-air assemblies, and operations over people inside moving vehicles are covered in the lessons below.

sub_units.title: Categories 1 and 2
sub_units.description: Compare Category 1 and Category 2 aircraft eligibility for operations over people.
sub_units.text_content:
Category 1 UA:
- Weigh 0.55 lbs (250 g) or less at takeoff, including everything attached.
- Have no exposed rotating parts that could lacerate human skin.
- No Declaration of Compliance (DoC) or Means of Compliance (MoC) is required.

Category 2 UA:
- Must not cause injury exceeding 11 ft-lb of kinetic energy.
- Must have no exposed rotating parts that could lacerate human skin and no safety defects.
- Must be listed on an FAA-accepted DoC and MoC.
- Must display Category 2 eligibility labeling and include manufacturer instructions.

The RPIC must verify these requirements before operating over people under Category 1 or 2.

sub_units.title: Categories 3 and 4, Sustained Flight, and Crowds
sub_units.description: Apply Category 3 and 4 requirements and restrictions on sustained flight over open-air assemblies.
sub_units.text_content:
Category 3 UA:
- Must not cause injury exceeding 25 ft-lb of kinetic energy.
- Must have no exposed rotating parts that could lacerate human skin and no safety defects.
- Requires FAA-accepted MoC and DoC, Category 3 labeling, and manufacturer instructions.
- Cannot fly over crowds or open-air assemblies unless inside a closed or restricted-access area where everyone is on notice that a drone may fly overhead, or unless the operation avoids sustained flight over non-participants (hovering, circling, or remaining above the same people). Operation over a person inside a vehicle or under a covered structure that provides protection is acceptable.

Category 4 UA:
- Must have an FAA airworthiness certificate issued under Part 21.
- Must be operated within approved Flight Manual limitations that do not prohibit flight over people.
- Requires maintenance, inspection, and recordkeeping per the approved data.

Sustained flight means hovering, circling, or repeatedly flying over the same group of people. An open-air assembly is generally a crowd of about 15–20 people gathered closely together.

Categories 1, 2, or 4: You may not conduct sustained flight over an open-air assembly unless the aircraft is broadcasting Remote ID (Standard Remote ID or broadcast module).

sub_units.title: Operation Over Moving Vehicles
sub_units.description: State when flight over people inside moving vehicles is permitted for each category.
sub_units.text_content:
Categories 1, 2, and 3: You may operate over a person inside a moving vehicle only if the UA remains within or over a closed- or restricted-access site, everyone inside moving vehicles at that site is on notice that a sUA may fly over them, and you do not maintain sustained flight over moving vehicles (brief transit only—no hovering, circling, or back-and-forth passes).

Category 4: The sUA must hold a Part 21 airworthiness certificate and be operated per the Flight Manual; operating limitations must not prohibit operations over human beings inside moving vehicles.

sub_units.title: Flying At Night Under Certain Conditions
sub_units.description: Explain when night operations are permitted without a waiver and how civil twilight lighting rules relate to anti-collision lighting.
sub_units.text_content: Night and civil twilight operations are allowed under Part 107 without a waiver when training and lighting requirements are met. Eligibility, civil twilight definitions, and manned-aircraft lighting recognition are covered in the first lesson below; hazards and mitigation strategies are in the second. No waiver is required unless you cannot meet these requirements.

sub_units.title: Night Eligibility, Civil Twilight, and Lighting
sub_units.description: Identify knowledge-test and recurrent training requirements, civil twilight operating rules, and anti-collision lighting standards for night flight.
sub_units.text_content:
As of April 21, 2021, night operations without a waiver are allowed when:
1) The RPIC has completed an initial knowledge test or recurrent training on or after April 6, 2021 (including the free online recurrent course at www.faasafety.gov); and
2) The sUA has anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate sufficient to avoid collision. The RPIC may dim lights if brightness would reduce safety, but lights must not be turned off under any circumstances.

You may not fly during civil twilight unless anti-collision lights meeting the above standard are on and remain on throughout the operation.

Night is the time period between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight. Morning civil twilight begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise. Evening civil twilight begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset. In Alaska, civil twilight is determined using the Air Almanac.

Understanding how vision works in low light supports safe night operations. Pilots use aircraft lighting to indicate direction and position: red on the left wing, green on the right wing, and white at the tail. Recognizing these lights helps you judge manned aircraft movement and maintain situational awareness near airports.

Night operations still require VLOS. Controlled airspace still requires authorization. All rules for flight over people still apply when flying at night.

sub_units.title: Night Flight Hazards and Mitigation
sub_units.description: Apply practical strategies to manage reduced visibility, depth perception, orientation, and battery effects during night sUAS operations.
sub_units.text_content:
Flying at night introduces hazards that may be absent or less noticeable during the day. You may struggle to see the drone, its orientation, obstacles, wildlife, and other aircraft. Depth perception decreases. Additional ground lighting may be needed.

Lighting and vision challenges:
- Avoid looking directly at bright lights.
- Use required anti-collision lights; prefer high-intensity strobe-style lights in cluttered lighting environments.
- Check ground lighting and add extra lighting near the landing area.
- Shift gaze 5–10° off center to reduce the night blind spot.
- Fly closer and lower than in daytime; inspect the site during daylight before the night operation.

VLOS challenges: Use multiple visual observers or VOs trained on night procedures; keep the aircraft lit and within VLOS.

Depth perception and situational awareness: Reduce speed; increase standoff distances; keep the aircraft within a shorter radius.

Circadian rhythm and fatigue: Avoid exhaustion and hypoglycemia.

Cold-night battery effects: Start with warmed batteries; reduce aggressive maneuvers; shorten flights; monitor battery more frequently.

Loss of orientation: Use bright position lighting (different colors on different arms); fly predictable patterns; avoid unnecessary rotation; land immediately if orientation is lost.

units.title: Airports, Airspace, and Data Sources
units.description: Build NAS and ATC context, use latitude and longitude for planning, and consult airport data sources and aeronautical charts before operating near airports. Airspace classifications and airport operating procedures are covered in later units.
units.text_content:
This unit is your orientation to flying near airports: how traffic fits into the National Airspace System, how ATC supports that traffic, how to locate positions with latitude and longitude, and how to find and use airport data (Chart Supplement, NOTAMs, ATIS) and aeronautical charts (sectional, TAC, legend, obstacles, MEF).

This unit does not teach every airspace class in depth—that is the next unit—and it does not cover airport traffic-pattern procedures—that comes in airport operations. Stay focused here on context plus finding and reading the data you need before you fly.

sub_units.title: Introduction to Air Traffic and the NAS
sub_units.description: Frame how busy U.S. air traffic, the National Airspace System, and ATC fit together before learning to locate positions and read airport data sources.
sub_units.text_content:
This section introduces the air-traffic context remote pilots need before reading charts or airport data. Start with how busy the system already is, then what the National Airspace System (NAS) includes, then what Air Traffic Control (ATC) does to keep traffic separated and flowing.

After this section you will learn latitude and longitude for locating positions, then the airport data sources and aeronautical charts you must review before flying near airports. Airspace class details (Class B, C, D, E, G, and special-use airspace) are covered in the next unit. Airport operating procedures (patterns, towered vs non-towered) come after that.

sub_units.title: Air Traffic by the Numbers
sub_units.description: Explain why integrating sUAS into the NAS requires a managed approach to safety and airspace integrity.
sub_units.text_content: Adding many small unmanned aircraft systems (sUAS) to the National Airspace System (NAS) is a complex challenge. A managed approach is necessary because of many variables and potential safety concerns. Maintaining the safety and integrity of U.S. airspace is essential as sUAS operations increase.

sub_units.title: National Airspace System (NAS)
sub_units.description: Identify the major components of the NAS and how each supports safe, efficient aviation operations.
sub_units.text_content:
The National Airspace System (NAS) is a network of airspace, navigation facilities, airports, technology, and regulations that enable safe and efficient air travel in the United States.

Major components include:
- Airspace Management: organizes controlled, uncontrolled, and special-use airspace.
- Communication Systems: link pilots and controllers.
- Navigation and Surveillance: radar, GPS, and related systems track aircraft and support navigation.
- Air Traffic Services: flight planning, weather services, and traffic flow management.
- Safety and Regulation: rules and oversight that keep operations safe.

sub_units.title: Air Traffic Control (ATC)
sub_units.description: State the primary purpose of ATC and the core services controllers provide to manned and unmanned operators.
sub_units.text_content:
The primary purpose of Air Traffic Control (ATC) is to prevent collisions between aircraft operating in the system and to organize and expedite the flow of traffic.

ATC services include:
- Instructions for flight paths, altitude changes, and landing or takeoff clearances.
- Separation of aircraft.
- Traffic flow management.
- Emergency assistance.
- Coordination across sectors.

sub_units.title: Navigation: Latitude and Longitude
sub_units.description: Locate positions with latitude and longitude, read chart tick marks and practice grids, convert decimal degrees to degrees-minutes-seconds, and check understanding with quiz figures.
sub_units.text_content:
Latitude and longitude are among the most reliable navigation references for pilots. Any point on Earth is defined by the intersection of a latitude line and a longitude line.

In the globe figure, parallels of latitude are shown as yellow lines (measured north or south of the equator), and meridians of longitude are shown as red lines (measured east or west of the Prime Meridian at Greenwich, England). The continental United States lies between about 25° and 49° N latitude and about 67° and 125° W longitude. Example: Chicago is approximately 42° N, 88° W.

On the Latitude and Longitude chart crop (Jacksonville area), the degree grid and minute tick marks are the chart’s printed black (and dashed) lines—not the yellow/red globe colors. Use those ticks to read whole degrees, 1′ marks, 10′ marks, and 30′ lines. The example airport Jacksonville Exec at Craig is at 30°20′ N, 81°31′ W.

On the Reading L & L lines figure (Sacramento area), yellow callout boxes label the same black chart ticks: longitude values increase going west, and latitude values increase going north. Do not treat the yellow boxes as the latitude lines themselves.

On the Points A–D practice grids, black squares mark minutes; red reference lines mark the labeled degree or half-degree. Find each red point by counting minutes from those references.

Format: Degrees are divided into 60 minutes; minutes may be divided into 60 seconds. Coordinates are written degrees (°), minutes (′), and seconds (″), with latitude first, then longitude. In many digital systems, north and east are positive; south and west are negative. For example, (39.72, -71.97) means 39.72° North and 71.97° West.

Decimal conversion (required for sectional chart work): Use the whole number as degrees; multiply the decimal portion by 60 for minutes; multiply the decimal portion of minutes by 60 for seconds.

JFK example: 40.6399° N, 73.7797° W → 40°38′23″ N, 73°46′47″ W (0.6399×60 = 38.39′; 0.39×60 ≈ 23″; 0.7797×60 = 46.78′; 0.78×60 ≈ 47″).

The sample L & L grids (no map) walk conversion and tick counting with worked answers under each grid. Use the Figure 1 and Figure 2 quiz pictures last to check that you can read coordinates without relying on the teaching callouts.

sub_units.title: Airports, Charts, and Data Sources
sub_units.description: List the mandatory sources remote pilots must review when planning operations within five miles of an airport.
sub_units.text_content:
If you plan to fly within five miles of an airport, review current airport data before the operation. Data includes communication frequencies, available services, closed runways, and airport construction.

The sources of information are:
- Aeronautical charts
- Chart Supplement U.S. (formerly Airport/Facility Directory)
- Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs)
- Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)

Detailed lessons for each source follow below; aeronautical chart types are covered in the next section.

sub_units.title: Chart Supplement U.S.
sub_units.description: Describe the Chart Supplement U.S. content, revision cycle, and how to use the legend sample for airport planning.
sub_units.text_content:
The Chart Supplement U.S. (formerly the Airport/Facility Directory) provides the most comprehensive information on an airport, including airports, heliports, and seaplane bases.

It is updated in print and digital formats and is revised every 56 days. Source: www.faa.gov/air_traffic/flight_info/aeronav

Information includes runway data and elevations, CTAF radio frequency, contact phone numbers, and weather sources. How to interpret entries is explained in the Chart Supplement "Legend Sample."

sub_units.title: Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs)
sub_units.description: Define NOTAMs, identify common reasons they are issued, and locate official NOTAM sources before flight.
sub_units.text_content:
A Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) is time-critical aeronautical information—temporary in nature or not known far enough in advance to publish in chart supplements or other operational publications. NOTAMs are disseminated immediately through the NOTAM system. Reviewing NOTAMs may change your decision to fly; use good judgment and common sense.

Reasons for NOTAMs include: hazards (air shows, parachute jumps, kite flying, rocket launches); flights involving dignitaries; inoperable lights on tall obstructions; temporary obstacles near airfields; and bird activity (BIRDTAM).

NOTAM sources:
- https://notams.aim.faa.gov/
- https://tfr.faa.gov/tfr3/?page=list
- www.1800wxbrief.com

Sample NOTAM (JFK crane) for study: !JFK 07/398 JFK OBST CRANE (ASN 2024-AEA-9387-OE) 404002N0734744W (1.8NM NNW JFK) 189FT (171FT AGL) FLAGGED AND LGTD 2507171151-2701151800
- !JFK: John F. Kennedy International Airport.
- 07/398: NOTAM number 398 issued in July.
- OBST CRANE: obstruction (crane) near JFK.
- 404002N0734744W: 40°40'02" N, 73°47'44" W.
- 1.8 NM NNW JFK: position relative to the airport.
- 189 FT (171 FT AGL): heights MSL and AGL.
- FLAGGED AND LGTD: marked and lighted.
- 2507171151-2701151800: effective times in UTC.

On the FAA knowledge test you are not required to fully decode complex NOTAM strings from memory; understand what each field represents and always check NOTAMs before flight.

sub_units.title: Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)
sub_units.description: Explain what ATIS broadcasts include, how often it is updated, and how pilots confirm they have current information with ATC.
sub_units.text_content:
The Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS) is a looped recording of weather and other information broadcast on a local frequency. It may include weather, runways in use, specific ATC procedures, and airport construction that could affect your plan.

ATIS is updated at least hourly and more often when conditions warrant. Each update receives a phonetic code named for that ATIS broadcast (for example, ATIS Alpha, then ATIS Bravo). Before contacting ATC, listen to ATIS and state the current code on initial contact (for example, "with information Bravo"—the standard radio phrase for the ATIS letter). This confirms you have current local weather and airport information without the controller repeating it. Use ATIS at departure and arrival airports when available.

sub_units.title: Aeronautical Charts
sub_units.description: Explain how aeronautical charts support remote pilot planning and how sectional and terminal area charts fit into the four airport data sources.
sub_units.text_content:
Aeronautical charts are the road map for pilots. They provide information remote pilots need about intended operating areas, including airport names, airport class, traffic patterns, radio frequencies, and elevations.

Aeronautical publications also serve as a learning guide for new pilots and a quick reference for experienced pilots. The FAA is the source for planning charts and Visual Flight Rules (VFR) and Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) publications, including training, planning, departure, en route, approach, and taxi charts.

The two chart types used most by drone operators under Part 107 are sectional charts and Terminal Area Charts (TACs).

During planning, determine whether your flight will be near an airport, review the sectional chart for that airport, and obtain airspace authorization when required.

Using aeronautical charts: charts include airspace information, navigational and procedural information, chart limits, culture (man-made features like cities, roads, railroads, and towers), hydrography (bodies of water), and relief (maximum elevation figures and contours). Other information includes airports: locations, runway details, lighting, and services.

sub_units.title: Sectional Charts
sub_units.description: Describe sectional chart coverage, scale, revision cycle, and what legend information pilots should verify before flight.
sub_units.text_content:
Sectional charts are the most common charts used by pilots today. They cover the entire United States and are named based on major cities shown on each chart.

Scale is 1:500,000. Charts provide airport data, navigational aids, airspace, and topography. Charts are revised semiannually, except Alaska sectional charts, which are revised annually.

Before flying, check the chart legend for other information you need, including air traffic control (ATC) frequencies and airspace details.

sub_units.title: Terminal Area Charts (TACs)
sub_units.description: Explain when Terminal Area Charts provide useful zoomed-in detail near busy airports and how TAC scale and revision cycles compare with sectionals.
sub_units.text_content:
Terminal Area Charts (TACs) cover the busiest airports and give a zoomed-in view of the surrounding area—for example, Class B airspace near a major city. The Miami TAC figure is one example of that detail.

TAC scale is 1:250,000, providing about twice the detail of a sectional chart. TACs are revised semiannually, except charts for the Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, which are revised annually. TACs do not cover the entire United States.

sub_units.title: Chart Legend, Supplement, and Airport Data
sub_units.description: Use the chart legend and Airmen Knowledge Testing Supplement to read airport data blocks, towered vs non-towered airport symbols, related airspace legend cues, and communication boxes.
sub_units.text_content:
Symbols and terms on the VFR Terms and VFR Sectional and TAC tabs in the Airmen Knowledge Testing Supplement, Appendix 1, are essential references. On the knowledge test you receive a supplement copy—you cannot use your own. A free PDF of the testing supplement is available at https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/training_testing/testing/supplements/sport_rec_private_akts.pdf. You should purchase a printed copy because you will have to use the one they supply on the test, and you cannot zoom in like you can on a computer or mobile device.

The first two figures break down a typical airport information block from the legend: name and identifiers, control tower (CT) and CTAF cues, ATIS, elevation, lighting, longest runway length, UNICOM, right-traffic (RP) notes, and related abbreviations.

Airport symbols: blue symbols indicate an airport with a control tower; magenta symbols indicate an airport without a control tower.

Example airport data. In the DFW and related example figures, read the airport name and location identifier, CT/ATIS/UNICOM frequencies, elevation, lighting, and runway length before operating nearby. Also note traffic pattern direction (left or right) when shown—it tells you where manned traffic will be relative to you. A small flag symbol marks a VFR checkpoint; expect higher air traffic volume in those areas.

The Sectional Aeronautical Chart legend figure collects airport colors/symbols, airport data layout, obstruction height format, and other chart keys in one place—use it with Appendix 1 when you study.

The airspace-information legend figures show how controlled and special-use airspace lines and shading appear on the chart (Class B/C/D/E cues and special-use boundaries). Full class rules are taught in the next unit; here the goal is recognizing the legend so you can find the right detail on a sectional.

Communication boxes are mainly used by manned aviation operations but remain testable knowledge for remote pilots. The communications-boxes figure shows heavy-line FSS boxes, thin-line remoted frequencies, receive-only (R) suffixes, and related status marks.

sub_units.title: Man-Made Obstacles on Sectional Charts
sub_units.description: Read man-made obstacle symbols on sectionals, including top=MSL / bottom=AGL labels, grouped triangle heights, and lighting marks.
sub_units.text_content:
Sectional charts depict man-made obstacles with symbols such as small triangles or tower icons (radio towers, wind turbines, and similar structures).

On the obstacle label in the Manmade obstacles figure (Fort Worth crop), the top number is MSL (mean sea level) and the bottom number in parentheses is AGL (above ground level). In the circled example, 1216 is MSL and 565 is AGL. Other circled labels on the same figure use the same stacked format.

When two or more triangles (grouped obstacles) appear close together, the height shown (MSL) is the highest of the group.

A lightning bolt or star above the symbol indicates the obstacle is lighted for night visibility.

Remote pilots must identify the highest relevant MSL height for the area and use AGL when it is provided to understand how tall the structure is above the ground.

sub_units.title: Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF)
sub_units.description: Define the Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF), how it is formatted on sectional charts, and how to use it for terrain and obstacle awareness.
sub_units.text_content:
The Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) is the highest elevation—terrain or man-made obstacle—within a chart quadrant of latitude and longitude (30' × 30', or 30 minutes by 30 minutes), plus a safety buffer.

MEF values are shown in hundreds of feet MSL, rounded up to the nearest hundred; the last two digits are omitted (for example, "35" means 3,500 feet MSL).

units.title: Airspace Classifications
units.description: Identify all airspace classifications used by remote pilots—controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other areas—and apply chart symbols, altitude references, and authorization requirements.
units.text_content:
This unit covers airspace categories, controlled classes A through G, chart-reading skills for the knowledge test, special use airspace, and other designated areas.

Lessons: an introduction with shape cues for the main classes; each controlled class with chart examples; Class E as one section (overview, E2 surface areas, and E3/E4 extensions); chart-question methodology; then special use and other airspace.

sub_units.title: Introduction and Airspace Classifications
sub_units.description: Identify the regulatory categories of airspace, chart symbols, and the controlled classes most relevant to remote pilots, including MSL versus AGL altitude references.
sub_units.text_content:
INTRO TO AIRSPACE CLASSIFICATIONS
AIRSPACE CATEGORIES
Airspace is broken into two categories—regulatory and nonregulatory—which are further broken down into controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other airspace.

Classification is based on complexity and concentration of aircraft movements, type of operations, level of safety required, and national and public interest.

Shape cues that help you recognize controlled classes: Class B and C look like an upside-down wedding cake; Class D looks like a cylinder and starts from the ground; Class E varies, but covers the entire United States at some level. Class G is uncontrolled airspace—not depicted on sectional charts—and no authorization is needed (G means go).

AIRSPACE INFORMATION
It is important to understand the various airspace symbols and the type of airspace you plan on operating in before flight. The All Airspace Classifications figure summarizes the classes you will study in this unit.

CONTROLLED AIRSPACE OVERVIEW
Controlled airspace is a generic term that covers the different classifications of airspace. It has defined dimensions within which air traffic control (ATC) service is provided.

Be sure to note whether MSL or AGL is used when determining altitude: Classes A, B, C, and D use MSL; Class E and G use MSL and AGL.

Airspace of concern to the remote pilot is:
- Class A — starts at 18,000 feet MSL and covers the entire U.S.
- Class B — busiest airports (upside-down wedding cake layers)
- Class C — mid-sized airports (also cake-like surface + shelf)
- Class D — small city airports (one cylinder-like layer from the surface)
- Class E (including surface areas and extensions) — least busy airports; covers the entire U.S. at some level
- Class G — uncontrolled; go when no other class applies

sub_units.title: Controlled Airspace Classes
sub_units.description: Summarize controlled airspace, MSL versus AGL references, and the classes most relevant to remote pilots.

sub_units.title: Class A Airspace
sub_units.description: Describe Class A vertical limits, IFR requirement, coastal coverage, and why it is not charted.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS A
Class A is the highest level of airspace. It extends from 18,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) up to and including flight level (FL600) (60,000 feet). The 60,000' altitude is shortened to 600 (the hundredths place). It includes airspace over water within 12 NM of the coast. All pilots must operate aircraft under instrument flight rules (IFR). Primary users are high-altitude commercial flights and long-haul aircraft. No markings are found on charts because its vertical boundaries are known and not charted.

sub_units.title: Class B Airspace
sub_units.description: Define Class B dimensions, structure, ATC authorization requirement, and solid blue chart markings.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS B AIRSPACE
Class B airspace extends from the surface to 10,000 feet mean sea level (MSL) around the busiest airports. It consists of a surface area and two or more layers, resembling an upside-down wedding cake. Think about how an aircraft lands or takes off from the airport—larger airports need more airspace.

Remote pilots must receive authorization from ATC before operating in Class B airspace. Markings are solid blue lines. Layer altitudes are shown in blue and charted in MSL, displayed as a fraction (for example 125/SFC and 125/30). The bottom number represents the floor and the top number represents the ceiling, both in hundreds of feet. The layer that starts at ground level is noted as SFC in the bottom portion of the fraction.

Class B Chart Examples:
CLASS B EXAMPLE — Atlanta, GA (ATL) (Hartsfield/Jackson)
Markings are solid blue lines. Layer altitudes are shown in blue. Charted in MSL and displayed as a fraction—for example 125/SFC and 125/30.

CLASS B EXAMPLE — Baltimore/Washington Intl Thurgood Marshall Airport
Markings are solid blue lines. Layer altitudes are shown in blue. Charted in MSL and displayed as a fraction—for example 100/SFC and 100/15.

sub_units.title: Class C Airspace
sub_units.description: Define Class C dimensions, tower and radar requirements, inner and outer rings, authorization, and magenta markings.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS C
Class C airspace normally extends from the surface to 4,000 feet (MSL). Airports in Class C have an operational control tower. They are not as busy as Class B but still important. Class C airspace is serviced by radar approach control and has instrument flight rules (IFR) operations.

Like Class B, it resembles an upside-down wedding cake: a surface area with a 5 nautical mile (NM) radius is typical, tailored to the airport. The outer circle is a 10 NM radius that extends from 1,200' to 4,000' MSL. Authorization is required before operating in Class C airspace. Markings are solid magenta lines. Layer altitudes are written in magenta.

Class C Chart Examples:
CLASS C EXAMPLE — Toledo Express (TOL)
Toledo Express has an operational control tower—a requirement for Class C. Markings are solid magenta lines. Layer altitudes are written in magenta.
- Inner Ring: Floor surface to ceiling of 4,700 feet MSL
- Outer Ring: Floor 2,000 feet MSL to ceiling 4,700 feet MSL

CLASS C EXAMPLE — Anchorage, Alaska (PANC)
- Inner core: Surface to 4,100' MSL within 5 NM
- Outer ring: 1,400' to 4,100' MSL
- Class E extensions for approach paths

sub_units.title: Class D Airspace
sub_units.description: Describe Class D dimensions, tower requirement, part-time reversion, authorization, and dashed blue markings.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS D
Class D airspace normally extends from the surface to 2,500' above the airport elevation MSL. It surrounds airports that have an operational control tower and is less busy than Class C airspace. Class D airspace is one layer from the surface (think of a cylinder) and is individually tailored. Some Class D areas have arrival extensions or departures for Class D or Class E, and some have a 5 NM radius around the airport.

If the control tower is part-time, the airspace reverts to Class E or G airspace. Remote pilots must receive ATC authorization before operating in Class D airspace. Markings are dashed blue lines. The airspace ceiling is indicated by a number in a dashed box; its altitude is given in hundreds of feet. The fraction format is not used because there is only one layer starting at the surface.

Class D Chart Example (kluk):
CLASS D — Cincinnati Municipal/Lunken Field Airport (KLUK)
Dashed blue line markings. The airspace ceiling is indicated by a number in a dashed box; its altitude is given in hundreds of feet.
- An outer ring marked 30 represents 3,000 feet MSL
- An area marked (-21) indicates up to but not including 2,100' MSL

sub_units.title: Class D with Class E Extension
sub_units.description: Recognize Class D combined with Class E extensions and apply communication and authorization requirements at Concord-Padgett (JQF).
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS D WITH A CLASS E EXTENSION — Concord-Padgett Regional Airport (JQF)
Class D is controlled airspace; pilots are required to communicate with air traffic control when the tower is operational. This example shows Class D airspace with a Class E extension depicted with magenta dashed lines.

Sample test question: (Refer to FAA-CT-8080-2H, Figure 23, area 3.) What is the floor of the Savannah Class E airspace at the shelf area (outer circle)? Use the chart-question steps lesson to work through figure-based airspace questions like this one.

sub_units.title: Class E
sub_units.description: Explain Class E purpose, vertical limits, default bases, federal airways, and how surface areas (E2) and extensions (E3/E4) fit the Class E model.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS E
Class E is the least busy controlled airspace. It is controlled airspace not classified as Class A, B, C, or D. A large amount of the airspace over the U.S. is Class E and provides sufficient airspace for the safe control of aircraft during IFR operations.

Class E extends up to, but not including, 18,000' MSL (the lower limit of Class A). All airspace above 60,000' MSL is Class E airspace. In areas where charts do not depict a Class E base, Class E begins at 14,500' MSL. In most areas, the Class E airspace base is 1,200 ft AGL. In some areas, the Class E airspace base is at the surface or 700 feet AGL.

Some Class E airspace begins at an MSL altitude instead of an AGL altitude. Federal Airways, shown as blue lines on a sectional chart, are usually found within Class E airspace. Remote pilots do not need ATC authorization to operate in Class E except when in Class E2. Class E airspace acts as a transition zone into other airspaces.

Class E airspace can change its classification based on certain conditions. For instance, at small airports with part-time control towers, the airspace changes from Class D to Class E after the tower closes.

Class E Chart Examples — 700' and 1,200' AGL:
CLASS E EXAMPLE — Shelby-Cleveland County Regional Airport (KEHO)
Class E airspace beginning at 700 feet above ground level (AGL), shown with a faded magenta line (vignette).

Class E airspace with the floor 1,200' or greater above the surface that abuts Class G is represented by a blue vignette. The faded side of the vignette represents the typical floor of 1,200 feet AGL.

sub_units.title: Class E2 Surface Areas
sub_units.description: Define Class E2 surface areas, authorization requirements, and chart markings using PUJ, MTJ, and Bethel (PABE) examples.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS E2 — Paulding Northwest Atlanta (PUJ)
Class E2 starts at the surface. It is typically circular and centered on the airport to contain instrument approach procedures. Prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC) is required.

CLASS E2 EXAMPLE — Montrose Rgnl (MTJ)
Dashed magenta lines with no intersecting lines indicate Class E airspace starting at the surface. The Class E transition area—a faded magenta vignette around the airport—indicates Class E airspace beginning at 700' AGL. Class G uncontrolled airspace exists below the Class E transition area, from the surface up to 700' AGL outside the dashed magenta lines.

BETHEL ALASKA (PABE) CLASS E2
Class E can appear even with a blue dashed line. It indicates controlled airspace beginning at the surface—it can be Class E or Class D. A blue dashed line is normally Class D, but if there is no operating control tower, the same line may be used for Class E. Bethel has no control tower; airspace starts at the surface and is controlled Class E.

sub_units.title: Class E3 and E4 Extensions
sub_units.description: Distinguish Class E3 and E4 extensions from Class E2 and state authorization requirements for each.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS E3
Class E3 is an extension to a Class C surface area. It extends Class E airspace from the surface to provide IFR approach or departure paths. Class E3 is depicted by dashed magenta lines extending from Class C. No ATC authorization is required in E3, but authorization is needed in adjacent Class C airspace.

CLASS E4
Class E4 is an extension of a Class D or Class E surface area. It differs from an E2 area because it is not centered on the airport but extends another designated surface area, typically to accommodate instrument approach and departure paths. No ATC authorization is needed in E4. A dashed magenta line separates the airspace. Class D airspace authorization from ATC is needed when operating in the Class D portion.

sub_units.title: Class G Airspace
sub_units.description: Define Class G as uncontrolled airspace, its typical vertical limits, and the fact that it is not charted.
sub_units.text_content:
CLASS G AIRSPACE
Class G airspace is uncontrolled airspace. Class G is anywhere that is not Class A, B, C, D, or E. In the U.S., Class G starts at the surface and goes up to where Class E airspace begins—usually 700 or 1,200 feet AGL. Class G airspace is not depicted on the sectional chart. No prior authorization is required to fly in Class G airspace.

sub_units.title: Answering Airspace and Chart Questions
sub_units.description: Apply a six-step method to answer FAA knowledge-test airspace questions using the testing supplement and chart legend.
sub_units.text_content:
STEPS TO ANSWER AIRSPACE AND CHART QUESTIONS
1. Read the question and identify what map or chart is needed.
2. Open the Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement for Sport, Recreational, and Private Pilots and locate the correct figure and area referenced in the question.
3. Find the airport or location in the question on that chart.
4. Use the Legend (Page 1) to determine the airspace classification and whether there is a control tower—blue = controlled airport (towered), magenta = non-towered airport.
5. Identify altitude references—Class A, B, C, and D airspace use MSL; Class E and G may use MSL or AGL.
6. Apply the chart information to the question and select the correct answer.

sub_units.title: Special Use Airspace
sub_units.description: Identify the six special use airspace types, planning considerations, and legend information for each area.
sub_units.text_content:
SPECIAL USE AIRSPACE
Special use airspace is designated for specific activities within a defined area. If you are not involved in those activities, you may face restrictions when entering this airspace. As part of your planning, confirm whether you can fly in the area.

Multiple types of special use airspace are listed in the legend of the Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement. The size, shape, floor, and ceiling of each area vary. Information in the legend includes radio frequencies used, active hours, affected altitudes on your sectional chart, and the controlling agency's contact information.

Special use airspace types include restricted areas, prohibited areas, warning areas, military operation areas (MOAs), alert areas, and controlled firing areas (CFAs).

sub_units.title: Restricted Areas
sub_units.description: Define restricted areas, active/inactive flight rules, hazards, and hatched blue R-chart markings.
sub_units.text_content:
RESTRICTED AREAS
Flight is possible with restrictions but not when active. Check active hours and affected altitudes on the sectional chart; it lists the controlling agency. These areas can contain hazards such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles. Flying in the area without authorization may be extremely hazardous. They are depicted with a hatched blue border and the letter R followed by a number. Ex: R-4806 W Nellis AFR Range Complex used for military training and testing.

sub_units.title: Prohibited Areas
sub_units.description: Define prohibited areas, their national-security purpose, and P-number chart symbols.
sub_units.text_content:
PROHIBITED AREAS
Aircraft of any kind is prohibited. These areas are established for national security. They are indicated on the chart with a "P" followed by a number such as "47" and special marking as shown in the legend. Examples include the DOE nuclear weapons facility in Amarillo, TX, Camp David, and the National Mall in Washington DC.

sub_units.title: Warning Areas
sub_units.description: Define warning areas over open water, legal jurisdiction limits, and W-number chart markings.
sub_units.text_content:
WARNING AREAS
Warning areas are similar to restricted areas, but the U.S. does not have sole jurisdiction over airspace over open waters. Legally, they cannot stop you from flying into a warning area. They contain activity that may be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft. They start 3 NM from the U.S. coastline over domestic or international waters. Sectional charts depict warning areas with a blue-hatched border and a "W" followed by a number.

sub_units.title: Military Operations Areas (MOAs)
sub_units.description: Explain why MOAs exist, how they are charted, when to check controlling-agency advisories, and how nonparticipating IFR traffic may be cleared through an active MOA.
sub_units.text_content:
MILITARY OPERATIONS AREAS (MOAs)
MOAs were established to separate military training activities from other aircraft traffic.

MOAs can have lower altitude limits due to activity. They are depicted with magenta markings like alert areas. MOAs appear on sectional, VFR terminal area, and en route low altitude charts with a name and are sometimes numbered.

Check advisories from the controlling agency before planning to operate near or through an MOA. When an MOA is in use, nonparticipating IFR traffic may be cleared through the MOA if IFR separation can be provided.

See the Gamecock example used for F-16 training.

sub_units.title: Alert Areas
sub_units.description: Define alert areas for high-volume training or unusual aerial activity and A-number chart markings.
sub_units.text_content:
ALERT AREAS
Alert areas are depicted on aeronautical charts with an "A" followed by a number (e.g., A-293). They are depicted with magenta markings like MOA areas. They may contain a high volume of pilot training or an unusual type of aerial activity. There are no requirements to enter alert areas, but pay attention when flying in alert areas.

Alert Area A-293 is west of Daytona Beach Intl.

sub_units.title: Controlled Firing Areas (CFAs)
sub_units.description: Define controlled firing areas and explain why activities must stop when nonparticipating aircraft approach.
sub_units.text_content:
CONTROLLED FIRING AREAS (CFA)
CFAs contain activities that, if not conducted in a controlled environment, could be hazardous to nonparticipating aircraft. The difference between CFAs and other special use airspace is that activities must be suspended when a spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout position indicates an aircraft might be approaching the area. CFAs are not listed on aeronautical charts since they do not cause a nonparticipating aircraft to change its flight path.

sub_units.title: Other Airspace Areas
sub_units.description: Describe advisories, routes, temporary restrictions, and security-related airspace beyond the main classifications.
sub_units.text_content:
OTHER AIRSPACE AREAS
Other airspace areas include Local Airport Advisory (LAA), Military Training Routes (MTRs), Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs), parachute jump aircraft operations, published VFR routes, Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSA), National Security Areas (NSA), and Air Defense Identification Zones (ADIZ).

sub_units.title: Local Airport Advisory (LAA)
sub_units.description: Describe local airport advisory services, frequencies, and weather data available from Flight Service.
sub_units.text_content:
LOCAL AIRPORT ADVISORY
An advisory service provided by Flight Service facilities, located on the landing airport, using a discrete ground-to-air frequency or the tower frequency when the tower is closed.

Services include local airport advisories, automated weather reporting with voice broadcasting, and a continuous Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS)/Automated Weather Observing Station (AWOS) data display, other continuous direct reading instruments, or manual observations available to the specialist.

sub_units.title: Military Training Routes (MTRs)
sub_units.description: Identify MTR naming conventions for VFR and IFR routes and recognize that military aircraft may exceed 250 knots below 10,000 feet.
sub_units.text_content:
MILITARY TRAINING ROUTES
Military Training Routes (MTRs) are routes that military aircraft fly during training. Military aircraft can exceed 250 knots below 10,000 feet.

- VFR routes (VR): MTRs with no segment above 1,500' are identified by four-digit numbers (e.g., VR1007) and flown under Visual Flight Rules. VFR routes are not ATC-controlled.
- IFR routes (IR): MTRs that include one or more segments above 1,500' AGL are identified by three or fewer digit numbers (e.g., IR21, VR207) and flown under Instrument Flight Rules. IFR routes are under ATC control.

sub_units.title: Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs)
sub_units.description: Explain TFR content as NOTAMs, common reasons TFRs are issued, and which TFRs appear on sectional charts.
sub_units.text_content:
TEMPORARY FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS (TFRS)
TFR areas relating to national security are indicated with a broken blue line. Note: only TFRs relating to national security are charted.

A TFR is a type of Notice to Airmen (NOTAM). It includes the location of the temporary restriction, time period, area in statute miles, altitudes affected, FAA coordination facility and telephone number, and reason for the restriction. The pilot should check NOTAMs as part of flight planning.

A TFR is an area where air travel is restricted due to a hazardous condition, a special event, or a general warning for the entire airspace. Reasons include:
- Protect persons and property in the air or on the surface from an existing or imminent hazard
- Provide a safe environment for the operation of disaster relief aircraft
- Prevent an unsafe congestion of aircraft above an incident or event (e.g., Super Bowl)
- Protect declared national disasters for humanitarian reasons in the State of Hawaii
- Protect the President, Vice President, or other public figures
- Provide a safe environment for space agency operations

sub_units.title: Parachute Jump Aircraft Operations
sub_units.description: Locate parachute jump operation information in the Chart Supplement U.S. and on sectional charts.
sub_units.text_content:
PARACHUTE JUMP AIRCRAFT OPERATIONS
Operations are published in the Chart Supplement U.S. Sites that are used frequently are depicted on sectional charts.

sub_units.title: Published VFR Routes
sub_units.description: Define published VFR routes for navigating complex airspace and identify where they are charted.
sub_units.text_content:
PUBLISHED VFR ROUTES
Published VFR routes are for transitioning around, under, or through some complex airspace. Terms include VFR flyway, VFR corridor, Class B airspace VFR transition route, and terminal area VFR route. They are found on VFR terminal area planning charts—for example, charts covering the New York City area.

sub_units.title: Terminal Radar Service Areas (TRSA)
sub_units.description: Define TRSAs, their radar-separation purpose, and solid grey line chart markings.
sub_units.text_content:
TERMINAL RADAR SERVICE AREAS (TRSA)
Terminal Radar Service Areas are areas where participating pilots can receive additional radar services. The purpose of the service is to provide separation between all IFR operations and participating VFR aircraft. TRSAs are depicted on sectional charts with a solid grey line.

sub_units.title: National Security Areas (NSA)
sub_units.description: Define national security areas, voluntary avoidance requests, and NOTAM-based flight prohibitions.
sub_units.text_content:
NATIONAL SECURITY AREAS (NSAS)
National Security Areas exist anywhere there is a requirement for increased security and safety of ground facilities. Flight in NSAs may be temporarily prohibited by regulation under the provisions of 14 CFR part 99. Prohibitions are disseminated via NOTAM. Pilots are requested to voluntarily avoid flying in the area.

sub_units.title: Air Defense Identification Zones (ADIZ)
sub_units.description: Define ADIZ purpose along the U.S. perimeter and recognize magenta dotted boundary markings.
sub_units.text_content:
AIR DEFENSE IDENTIFICATION ZONES (ADIZ)
An Air Defense Identification Zone surrounds the country's perimeter, protecting the country from unknown aircraft. The government treats unidentified aircraft entering the ADIZ as possible threats and may intercept them with military aircraft. Sectional charts depict ADIZ boundaries with a magenta line with dots.

units.title: AIRPORT OPERATIONS
units.description: Introduce airport categories and towered/non-towered radio practices, then apply runway orientation, manned traffic patterns, runway position and heading examples, airport signs and markings, SIDA security, and wildlife hazard rules.
units.text_content:
This unit covers how airports are categorized and controlled, how runways are numbered and oriented, how manned traffic patterns work, how to interpret runway position and heading calls on CTAF, how to read airport signs and markings, and how security (SIDA) and wildlife rules affect remote pilots.

Lessons follow that sequence: intro to airport operations, runways, traffic patterns, runway position and heading examples, signs/markings/security, then wildlife hazards.

sub_units.title: Intro to Airport Operations
sub_units.description: Identify FAA legal airport categories, distinguish towered from non-towered airports, and explain UNICOM and CTAF radio practices before runway and pattern lessons.
sub_units.text_content:
Airport categories as defined by law:
