- Commercial Service Airports: Publicly owned, with at least 2,500 passenger boardings per year, including international flights stopping for non-traffic purposes (such as refueling).

- Cargo Service Airports: Served by aircraft transporting only cargo when total cargo weight exceeds 100 million pounds per year.

- Reliever Airports: FAA-designated airports intended to reduce congestion at commercial service airports.

- General Aviation Airports: All remaining airports not in the categories above. They form the largest group in the U.S. airport system.

Two types of airports exist based on operational control: towered and non-towered.

Within those categories you will find:
- Civil airports for the general public.
- Military and federal government airports.
- Private airports not open to the general public.

Facilities can include seaplane bases, heliports, tilt-rotor sites, and any area used or intended for use as an airport.

Towered airports have an operating control tower coordinating traffic on the ground and in the pattern.

UNICOM is a non-government station that provides airport information (weather, wind, runway in use). UNICOM may serve both towered and non-towered airports.

Non-towered airports do not have an operating control tower. Two-way radio is not required by regulation for all aircraft but is strongly recommended for safety. Pilots must operate with extra caution. Pilots announce position and intentions on the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF). CTAF is often the same as UNICOM but may instead be MULTICOM, Flight Service (FSS), or a tower frequency when the tower is closed—always verify the published frequency on the sectional chart or Chart Supplement.

sub_units.title: Runways: Surface Aids, Hazards, and Orientation
sub_units.description: Interpret runway surface navigational aids and describe magnetic runway numbering, including parallel runway designations and takeoff-and-landing hazards.
sub_units.text_content:
It is essential to understand signs, markings, and lights used on airports as surface navigational aids. These aids include the airport diagram or layout, runways in use, and the direction of departing and arriving aircraft.

Takeoff and landing are generally the most hazardous phases of flight. Low altitude and low airspeed leave little margin for error. Wind shear, crosswinds, fog, and low visibility are especially critical near the ground; sudden wind changes can destabilize an aircraft during landing or takeoff.

Runway orientation: Runways are aligned with the prevailing wind for better lift and control. The runway designation is the magnetic heading rounded to the nearest 10 degrees and shortened to two digits (for example, 273° magnetic becomes Runway 27). Opposite ends of the same physical runway differ by 180° (Runway 27 on one end, Runway 9 on the other).

Runway numbers range from 01 to 36, representing compass headings in 10-degree increments. Parallel runways add letters: L (left), C (center), R (right). For example, two parallel runways aligned with 090° magnetic are designated 09L and 09R.

sub_units.title: Traffic Patterns for Manned Aircraft
sub_units.description: Describe standard VFR traffic pattern flow, typical pattern altitudes near airports, and entry, downwind, final, and departure procedures.
sub_units.text_content:
Airports use a standard traffic pattern to organize takeoffs and landings. The pattern may differ when a control tower assigns non-standard flows, when terrain or obstacles require changes, or when pilots deviate for safety. Never assume every aircraft is flying the published left-hand pattern; if manned traffic is nearby, landing the sUAS until the area is clear may be the safest option.

Even though many propeller aircraft cruise at higher altitudes, they descend through lower altitudes near airports. On approach or departure paths, aircraft may be at roughly 500 to 1,500 feet AGL several miles from the field. Common pattern altitudes for light propeller aircraft are about 600 to 1,500 feet AGL.

Patterns are normally left-hand unless ATC assigns otherwise or the chart shows a right pattern with the (RP) symbol. Left-hand patterns are not specially labeled on the chart.

Significant pattern items:
- Enter the pattern in level flight, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude.
- 1,000 feet AGL is the recommended pattern altitude unless another altitude is published.
- Maintain pattern altitude until abeam the approach end of the landing runway on the downwind leg.
- Complete the turn to final at least one-quarter mile from the runway.
- After takeoff or go-around, continue straight ahead until past the departure end of the runway.
- If remaining in the pattern, begin the turn to crosswind beyond the departure end of the runway, within 300 feet of pattern altitude.
- If leaving the pattern, continue straight out or exit with a 45-degree turn beyond the departure end after reaching pattern altitude.

sub_units.title: Runway Position and Heading Examples
sub_units.description: Calculate aircraft magnetic heading on downwind from the runway number and determine relative position from CTAF position reports at a non-towered airport.
sub_units.text_content:
When you monitor the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF) at a non-towered airport, pilots self-announce position and intentions. Use runway magnetic alignment and standard traffic pattern geometry to interpret those calls.

Downwind heading (opposite the landing runway direction):
- Runway 18 or less: treat the runway number as tens of degrees, then add 180°. Example: Runway 12 → 120° + 180° = 300° downwind heading.
- Runway greater than 18: treat the runway number as tens of degrees, then subtract 180°. Example: Runway 24 → 240° − 180° = 60° downwind heading.

Example 1 — Left downwind Runway 16: landing direction is 160° magnetic; downwind is 160° + 180° = 340°, roughly northwest.

Example 2 — Midfield left downwind Runway 13. See figure runway 13.

Example 3 — Midfield left downwind Runway 4. See figure runway 4.

Example 4 — Left downwind Runway 12: downwind heading = 120° + 180° = 300°. See attached runway 12.

Example 5 — Left downwind Runway 24: downwind heading = 240° − 180° = 60°. See attached runway 24.

Example 6 — Short final Runway 18: the aircraft is on final aligned with Runway 18 (magnetic course 180° toward the runway). See image for runway 18.

sub_units.title: Airport Signs, Markings, and Security
sub_units.description: Read airport location and mandatory instruction signs, direction and holding markings, and Security Identification Display Area (SIDA) rules for operations on airport property.
sub_units.text_content: This section covers the surface signs and markings you must recognize near runways and taxiways, then airport security (SIDA) rules if your operation takes you onto airport property. Wildlife hazards are covered in the next lesson.

sub_units.title: Airport Location and Mandatory Instruction Signs
sub_units.description: Recognize location signs and mandatory instruction signs on airport movement areas and state when pilots must stop for ATC clearance.
sub_units.text_content:
Location signs have a black background with yellow letters and identify a taxiway or runway location.

Mandatory instruction signs have a red background with white letters. They mark locations where pilots must stop unless cleared by ATC—effectively a "do not enter" until cleared. They appear at runway intersections, critical areas, and other restricted zones.

Aircraft must not pass a mandatory instruction sign or associated holding position until ATC clears the movement.

sub_units.title: Direction, ILS Holding, and Runway Holding Markings
sub_units.description: Identify direction and destination signs, ILS critical area holding requirements, and runway holding position markings at taxiway and runway intersections.
sub_units.text_content:
Direction and destination signs have yellow backgrounds with black text and arrows and guide pilots to runways, terminals, cargo areas, and other airport locations.

ILS critical area holding position: When the ILS critical area is active—usually in low visibility—pilots must hold short as marked until the area is inactive or ATC clears the movement.

Runway holding position marking consists of two solid lines and two broken lines across the full width of the taxiway or runway. When approaching from the side with the continuous lines, do not cross without ATC clearance. These markings appear next to holding position signs at taxiway and runway intersections (for example, holding short of Runway 15 with Runway 33 to the right). Do not proceed beyond the holding position until cleared by ATC.

sub_units.title: Airport Security (SIDA)
sub_units.description: Explain Security Identification Display Area (SIDA) requirements and badge and movement rules under 49 CFR Part 1542.
sub_units.text_content:
If a drone operation requires you to enter airport property, determine whether that area is a Security Identification Display Area (SIDA).

Inside a SIDA you must wear a visible airport-issued identification badge and follow airport and TSA procedures under 49 CFR Part 1542. Movement in a SIDA without a displayed badge is prohibited.

sub_units.title: Wildlife Hazards Near Airports
sub_units.description: State reporting options for wildlife strikes, prohibitions on harassing wildlife, and immediate actions when wildlife threatens the operation.
sub_units.text_content:
Wildlife strikes are a serious hazard to manned aircraft. Remote pilots must not attract wildlife or increase strike risk near airports.

If your small unmanned aircraft collides with wildlife, you are not required to report it to the FAA, but you may report voluntarily to the FAA Wildlife Strike Database.

Harassing wildlife violates FAA policy and environmental laws. If you observe wildlife near your operation, land immediately and reassess before continuing.

units.title: WEATHER
units.sub_title: Aviation Weather Sources, Observations (METAR), and Forecasts (TAF)
units.description: Cover essential aviation weather services, how to read surface observation reports like METAR, and how to use key forecast products such as TAF, SIGMET, and AIRMET for safe flight planning.
units.text_content:
Weather is a critical part of preflight planning, requiring knowledge of specialized aviation weather sources, real-time observation reports, and various forecast products to ensure flight safety and informed decision-making.

Weather Services is a collaborative effort involving the National Weather Service (NWS), Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Defense (DOD), and other aviation organizations and individuals. Weather can vary greatly depending on location and altitude. Aviation weather reports are available at www.aviationweather.gov and 1800wxbrief.com. Weather forecasts are not 100% accurate but are increasingly reliable, using scientific research and computer models to identify patterns, trends, and characteristics of weather systems. This information supports informed decision-making for flight planning and safety.

sub_units.title: Surface Aviation Weather Observations
sub_units.text_content:
Surface Aviation Weather Observations include data from both government-operated and privately contracted facilities, providing real-time, localized weather data collected at ground stations across the US. Automated Weather Observing Systems (AWOS) and Automated Surface Observing Systems (ASOS) play major roles in data collection. AWOS is a collection of weather sensors that must meet FAA standards to be able to report weather factors. A Surface Observation Report contains:
  • Type of report (routine or special)
  • Station identifier (airport code or location)
  • Date and time of the observation
  • Modifier
  • Wind speed and direction
  • Visibility (horizontal distance pilots can see)
  • Runway Visual Range (RVR)
  • Weather phenomena
  • Sky condition
  • Temperature and dew point
  • Altimeter reading (atmospheric pressure)
  • Remarks
sub_units.description: Describe real-time, localized weather data sources, including AWOS and ASOS, and the general content of a surface observation report.

sub_units.title: Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) Decoding
sub_units.text_content:
Aviation Weather Reports provide accurate, current depictions of weather conditions to help pilots make informed decisions.

The METAR (Aviation Routine Weather Report) is the standard international format for surface weather observations, typically issued hourly.

The SPECI is a special METAR issued between routine reports when significant weather changes occur.

PIREP: Pilot Weather Report — Provided by pilots in flight to report the actual weather conditions encountered.

The report begins with the Type of report: METAR (regular) or SPECI (special report). This is followed by the Station identifier, a 4-letter code to identify airports and other aviation facilities. The Date & time of report is a 6-digit group (date + time) given in Zulu time (UTC), followed by 'Z'. The Modifier, if present, denotes an automated source ('AUTO') or a corrected report ('COR').

Wind is reported with five digits unless the speed is greater than 99 knots, in which case it is reported with six digits. The first three digits are direction; the last two digits are speed (three digits when speed exceeds 99 knots). Wind is reported with direction (first three digits, blowing from in tens of degrees) and speed (last two or three digits) in knots. If the wind direction is variable, 'VRB' is used. Gusts are indicated by 'G' followed by the peak gust (e.g., G26KT). Visibility is reported in statute miles ('SM').

Weather is broken down into Qualifiers (intensity: light (-), moderate ( ), heavy (+), and proximity: 'VC' for 5–10 miles from the airport) and Descriptors (describing precipitation or obscurations). Sky condition is reported with amount (in eighths), height (3-digit number in hundreds of feet AGL), and type (e.g., TCU or CB). Types of clouds, specifically towering cumulus (TCU) or cumulonimbus (CB), are reported with their height. 'VV' (vertical visibility) is used if clouds cannot be seen due to fog or heavy precipitation.

Air Temperature and Dew Point are always given in °C. Temperatures below 0 °C are preceded by 'M' (Minus). The Altimeter setting is inches of mercury ('Hg') in a four-digit group, preceded by 'A'. Remarks start with 'RMK' and include various additional data like pressure information ('PRESRR' or 'PRESFR') and automated station maintenance indicators.
sub_units.description: Decode the METAR format, covering report type (METAR/SPECI), PIREPs, station identifiers, time conventions, wind reporting, visibility, sky condition, and temperature/altimeter settings.

sub_units.title: Aviation Weather Forecast Products
sub_units.text_content: Forecasts are essential for preflight planning. Pilots should be familiar with the various types of forecast products that provide anticipated weather conditions for specific areas and altitudes.
sub_units.description: Identify the weather forecast products essential for flight planning, including TAF, SIGMET, AIRMET, and winds/temperatures aloft.

sub_units.title: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) and Aviation Area Forecast (FA)
sub_units.text_content: The TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) is a forecast for a specific airport (usually larger ones), covering expected weather within a 5-mile radius, valid for 24 or 30 hours and updated four times daily (0000Z, 0600Z, 1200Z, and 1800Z). TAFs use the same descriptors and abbreviations as in the METAR report. The FA (Aviation Area Forecast) is a broad regional forecast.
sub_units.description: State TAF coverage, duration, and update frequency, and explain the regional role of the Aviation Area Forecast (FA).

sub_units.title: SIGMET and Convective SIGMET (WST)
sub_units.text_content: SIGMET (Significant Meteorological Information) advisories are issued for severe weather hazards (e.g., turbulence, volcanic ash). Convective SIGMETs (WST) are issued specifically for severe thunderstorms producing surface winds greater than 50 knots, hail ¾ inch or larger, or the presence of tornadoes, or heavy precipitation affecting 40% or more of an area at least 3,000 square miles in size. They are relevant to all aircraft for safety and preflight planning.
sub_units.description: Explain the hazards covered by SIGMETs and the specific conditions that trigger a Convective SIGMET (WST).

sub_units.title: AIRMET and Winds/Temperatures Aloft (FB)
sub_units.text_content: AIRMET (Airman’s Meteorological Information) advisories are for less severe weather conditions (e.g., moderate turbulence or icing). The FB (Winds and Temperatures Aloft Forecast) provides wind direction, speed, and temperature at various altitudes, which is crucial for determining flight path efficiency and conditions at altitude.
sub_units.description: Distinguish AIRMET (moderate conditions) from the FB winds and temperatures aloft forecast, and explain when each is used.

sub_units.title: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) Decoding
sub_units.text_content:
The TAF provides essential forecast information for specific airports and uses a coded structure that must be carefully decoded to understand the expected weather conditions.

The TAF includes the Type of report (Routine TAF or Amended TAF AMD), the ICAO station identifier (4-digit code, same as a METAR), and the Date and time of origin (6-number code in UTC/Zulu). The first two digits are the date, and the last 4 are the time in UTC.

The TAF Valid period dates and times (e.g., 0812/0912) indicate the forecast's duration. This is followed by the core forecast elements: Forecast wind (five-digit group), Forecast visibility (in statute miles, 'P6SM' for greater than six miles), Forecast significant weather, and Forecast sky condition (same format as METAR, but only Cumulonimbus (CB) clouds are forecast in this section).

The Forecast change group indicates expected significant weather changes. 'FM' (From) is used when a rapid and significant change is expected (usually within an hour). 'TEMPO' (Temporary) is for temporary fluctuations of weather expected to last less than 1 hour. 'PROB30' or 'PROB40' (Probability) is a percentage describing the probability of thunderstorms and precipitation, but this group is not used for the first 6 hours of a 24-hour forecast.
sub_units.description: Decode the structure and content of a TAF report, including the valid period, wind, visibility, and forecast change groups like FM and TEMPO.

units.title: WEATHER EFFECTS ON AIRCRAFT PERFORMANCE
units.sub_title: Understanding Weather's Impact on sUAS Operations
units.description: Explain how atmospheric pressure, density, temperature, humidity, wind, stability, clouds, storms, fronts, and mountain weather affect sUAS performance so you can plan flights and decide when conditions exceed safe or regulatory limits.
units.text_content:
This unit connects weather to aircraft performance and risk. Pilots cannot control the weather—only their decisions. Every aircraft has weather limits set by the manufacturer; exceeding those limits increases the chance of loss of control, crashes, injury, or property damage. If weather exceeds what the aircraft can safely handle, do not fly. Routine jobs (for example, inspecting a roof) should be delayed when conditions are poor; only missions that truly justify it (for example, searching for a child whose life may be in danger) may warrant accepting higher weather risk. Most operations do not justify high weather risk. Pilots care about weather because it changes air density, which affects lift, thrust, stability, and battery endurance.

Weather is the current condition of the atmosphere at a specific time and place. It includes temperature, wind, atmospheric pressure, moisture (humidity and precipitation), and the clouds and precipitation those ingredients produce. Weather happens because the sun heats the Earth unevenly; uneven heating causes air to move. Moving air transports heat and moisture and is the engine behind changing conditions at the surface and aloft.

The lessons that follow build from pressure, density, and humidity through wind, atmospheric stability, inversions and moisture/icing, hazardous clouds and thunderstorms, fronts, mountain flying, and Part 107 ceiling and visibility minimums.

sub_units.title: Air Pressure, Density, Humidity, and Performance
sub_units.description: Explain how pressure and density change with altitude, apply density altitude to sUAS performance, and describe how pressure patterns and humidity further change density and performance.
sub_units.text_content: This section covers how air pressure and density change with altitude, how density altitude predicts sUAS performance in high-hot-humid conditions, and how pressure patterns and humidity further reduce density and performance. The lessons below start with pressure and density fundamentals, then density altitude, then pressure, humidity, and performance.

sub_units.title: Air Pressure and Density Fundamentals
sub_units.description: Define air pressure and air density, identify standard sea-level atmospheric values, and explain why pressure and density decrease with altitude.
sub_units.text_content:
Air pressure is the weight of the air above you caused by gravity. More air above you produces higher pressure, and less air above you produces lower pressure. As altitude increases, pressure decreases.

Pressure can be reported in inches of mercury (inHg) or millibars (mb). Standard sea-level atmosphere references are 29.92 inHg (1,013.2 mb) and 59°F (15°C).

Air density is the amount of air molecules in a given volume. As altitude increases and pressure drops, density also drops. High-density air (thick air) improves lift and propeller efficiency; low-density air (thin air) reduces lift and thrust.

sub_units.title: Density Altitude and Performance
sub_units.description: Define pressure altitude and density altitude and apply the high-hot-humid concept to predict reductions in sUAS lift, climb, propeller efficiency, and battery endurance.
sub_units.text_content:
Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature; it is the altitude in the standard atmosphere that corresponds to the current air density. Pressure altitude is the altitude shown when the altimeter is set to 29.92 inHg.

Standard temperature is 15°C at sea level and decreases about 2°C (3.5°F) per 1,000 feet. If actual temperature is above standard, density altitude increases.

High altitude, high temperature, and high humidity all reduce density. Exam mindset: mountains, summer heat, and humid conditions all point to lower density and higher density altitude.

Operational effect: high density altitude means reduced lift, reduced climb capability, reduced propeller efficiency, and shorter battery endurance. Lower density altitude means better performance.

sub_units.title: Pressure, Humidity, and Performance
sub_units.description: Explain how pressure and humidity influence density and weather behavior, including compressibility, relative humidity, and why pressure changes with altitude are usually the dominant density driver.
sub_units.text_content:
Pressure and density are linked because air is a compressible fluid. Increasing pressure compresses a given volume of air and raises density; decreasing pressure allows expansion and lowers density. Pressure can change by changing the number of molecules in a volume or by changing molecular energy (temperature). In the real atmosphere, both temperature and pressure usually decrease with altitude, but pressure typically decreases faster, so density usually decreases with altitude.

Pressure patterns also signal broad weather behavior. Low pressure often supports rising air, cooling, cloud formation, and less stable weather. High pressure usually supports sinking air, warming, and generally clearer, more stable conditions.

Humidity is the amount of water vapor in air. Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapor present compared with the maximum the air can hold at that temperature. Warm air can hold more water vapor than cold air. Dry air is 0% relative humidity; saturated air is 100%; 50% relative humidity means the air contains half of the moisture it could hold at that temperature.

Water vapor weighs less than the main dry-air gases. Approximate densities: water vapor (H₂O) ~0.80 g/L, oxygen (O₂) ~1.43 g/L, and nitrogen (N₂) ~1.25 g/L. Replacing oxygen and nitrogen with more water vapor makes the air lighter and less dense. Practical result: higher humidity lowers air density and performance, raises density altitude, and means less air for the propellers to push.

sub_units.title: Wind, Turbulence, and Severe Wind Hazards
sub_units.description: Explain how terrain, structures, open terrain, and weather systems create turbulence, wind shear, and microbursts, and apply operational precautions to avoid exceeding aircraft limits.
sub_units.text_content:
Wind effects depend on obstacles, terrain, and weather systems. Turbulence increases with obstacle size and wind speed and can degrade aircraft stability and image quality for video and photography missions.

Use extra caution near open fields and water. With fewer obstacles to slow it, wind may be stronger than in nearby sheltered areas, and gusts may exceed manufacturer limits. If observed or forecast wind exceeds aircraft limits, do not fly.

The lessons below cover obstacle and terrain-induced turbulence, low-level wind shear and microbursts, then practical go/no-go wind decisions.

sub_units.title: Obstacle and Terrain-Induced Turbulence
sub_units.description: Identify terrain and structure-driven turbulence patterns, including windward versus leeward mountain flow and building-corner turbulence, and apply safe operating cautions.
sub_units.text_content:
Obstacles create turbulence, and turbulence strength depends on obstacle size and wind velocity. Expect disturbed air around structures, tree lines, mountains, bluffs, and canyons.

Mountain terrain often provides smoother lifting flow on the windward side, but increasingly turbulent descending flow on the leeward side that can push an aircraft toward terrain.

Around buildings, wind often cannot follow sharp corners cleanly and separates, creating turbulent eddies and gusts on the leeward side.

sub_units.title: Low-Level Wind Shear and Microbursts
sub_units.description: Define wind shear and microbursts, identify common triggers, and explain why these hazards are especially dangerous for low-altitude sUAS operations.
sub_units.text_content:
Wind shear is a sudden change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance. It can occur at any altitude and may create updrafts, downdrafts, and abrupt horizontal wind shifts. It is especially dangerous close to the ground where recovery margins are small.

Wind shear is associated with frontal systems, thunderstorms, temperature inversions, and strong upper-level winds (often greater than 25 knots).

Microbursts are intense localized downdrafts from convective weather that spread outward at the surface and can force small aircraft downward rapidly.

sub_units.title: Operational Wind Risk Decisions
sub_units.description: Apply practical go/no-go decisions for wind by comparing observed and forecast conditions with manufacturer limits, terrain effects, and mission requirements.
sub_units.text_content: Before launch, compare forecast and observed wind and gust values to manufacturer limits. Reassess at the site because local terrain and structures can make actual winds much stronger than regional reports. When operating near mountains, ridges, buildings, or shoreline/open-field transitions, expect changing wind direction and turbulence. If conditions approach limits, reduce exposure, increase standoff from obstacles, or delay/cancel the mission.

sub_units.title: Atmospheric Stability
sub_units.description: Describe how moisture and temperature determine atmospheric stability and connect unstable versus stable air to convective currents, turbulence, and cloud type.
sub_units.text_content:
Convective currents form when uneven heating causes warm air to rise (updrafts) and cooler air to sink (downdrafts), creating bumpy, turbulent flight. Stability depends on the air's ability to resist vertical motion. When the atmosphere is unstable, vertical motions grow stronger and can produce significant turbulence, extensive vertical clouds, and severe weather.

The combination of moisture and temperature determines stability. Warm, moist air (for example summer tropical air) often supports unstable conditions and daily thunderstorm risk with cumuliform (vertically developed) clouds. Cool, dry air tends to be very stable, resists vertical motion, and generally supports clearer weather with layered stratiform clouds.

sub_units.title: Temperature Inversions, Dew Point, and Structural Icing Hazards
sub_units.description: Explain temperature inversions and visibility effects, the temperature–dew point relationship and condensation on aircraft surfaces, and the two required conditions for structural icing including aerodynamic cooling near freezing.
sub_units.text_content: This section covers temperature inversions that trap moisture and pollutants, dew point and condensation effects on aircraft performance, then structural icing hazards. In-flight icing requires visible moisture and a surface at or below freezing, including near-freezing cases where aerodynamic cooling drops local temperature. The lessons below cover inversions, dew point/condensation, then structural icing.

sub_units.title: Temperature Inversions
sub_units.description: Define temperature inversions, contrast them with the normal lapse rate, and explain how surface and frontal inversions affect turbulence and visibility.
sub_units.text_content:
Under normal conditions, temperature decreases with altitude as air rises and expands. In a temperature inversion, temperature increases with altitude.

Inversion layers are often shallow, smooth, and stable near the surface. Air at the top of the layer acts as a lid that traps weather and pollutants below. Surface-based inversions commonly form on clear, cool nights when the ground cools the nearby air. A low-level inversion (warmer air above cooler air near the ground) can feel stable while still trapping pollution and supporting fog or smog. Frontal inversions occur when warm air spreads over cooler air, or cooler air is forced under warmer air, and can worsen flight conditions.

When relative humidity is high, inversions can contribute to clouds, fog, haze, or smoke and diminished visibility in the inversion layer.

sub_units.title: Dew Point and Condensation
sub_units.description: Define dew point and explain how temperature–dew point spread relates to relative humidity and condensation products that can degrade sUAS performance.
sub_units.text_content:
Dew point is the temperature at which air is saturated. The closer air temperature is to dew point, the higher the relative humidity.

When temperature cools to dew point, moisture condenses into fog, dew, frost, clouds, rain, or snow depending on conditions. Dew or frost on aircraft surfaces adds weight and disrupts airflow, reducing lift and performance.

sub_units.title: Structural Icing
sub_units.description: Identify structural icing hazards, the two required icing conditions, and why aerodynamic cooling makes near-freezing operations risky.
sub_units.text_content:
Structural icing is dangerous because ice increases drag, reduces lift, and adds weight.

Two conditions are required for structural icing in flight: the aircraft must be in visible moisture, and the surface where moisture strikes must be 0°C or colder.

Aerodynamic cooling can reduce local surface temperature below ambient, allowing icing even when outside air temperature is slightly above freezing.

sub_units.title: Clouds and Thunderstorm Life Cycle
sub_units.description: Identify hazardous cloud types and fully describe the thunderstorm life cycle, including stage-specific hazards such as turbulence, wind shear, hail, lightning, and microbursts.
sub_units.text_content: This section covers hazardous cloud types for small UAS—especially cumulonimbus and standing lenticular clouds—then the thunderstorm life cycle through cumulus, mature, and dissipating stages. Multicell storms may contain different stages at the same time. The lessons below identify the cloud types, then walk the stage-specific hazards for go/no-go decisions.

sub_units.title: Hazardous Cloud Types
sub_units.description: Recognize cumuliform, cumulonimbus, and standing lenticular clouds and explain the specific turbulence and severe-weather hazards each signals for sUAS operations.
sub_units.text_content:
Cumuliform clouds indicate vertical development and potential convective turbulence. Cumulonimbus clouds are highly hazardous, with severe turbulence, lightning, hail, heavy precipitation, and possible tornado activity.

Standing lenticular altocumulus clouds form in mountain waves, often have smooth polished edges, and can appear nearly stationary even while strong winds and severe lee-side turbulence are present.

sub_units.title: Thunderstorm Life Cycle
sub_units.description: Explain cumulonimbus storm evolution through cumulus, mature, and dissipating stages and identify the key hazard cues in each stage for go/no-go decisions.
sub_units.text_content:
Thunderstorms evolve through three stages:

Cumulus stage: dominated by strong updrafts and rapid vertical growth (often greater than 3,000 ft/min). Water droplets grow as rising air carries moisture upward; icing risk can develop aloft where supercooled liquid water exists. As droplets grow heavier and begin to fall, cold rain can drag air downward; when a strong updraft and new downdraft coexist, the storm transitions to the mature stage.

Mature stage: begins when precipitation starts and strong downdrafts develop alongside updrafts. Cold rain keeps the downdraft colder than surrounding air so it accelerates downward; downdraft speeds may exceed 2,500 ft/min. Down-rushing air spreads outward at the surface, producing strong gusty winds, a sharp temperature drop, and a rapid pressure rise. The leading edge of that surface wind surge is the plow wind; its first wave is the "first gust." Updrafts reach maximum strength while updrafts and downdrafts together create severe vertical wind shear. This is the most dangerous phase for aviation and UAS operations: turbulence, wind shear, hail, lightning, microbursts, and strong downdrafts.

Dissipating stage: downdrafts dominate and then weaken. Precipitation decreases and the cell breaks apart; once downdrafts cease, the storm cell has dissipated and remaining clouds are generally less hazardous.

sub_units.title: Fronts, Mountain Flying, and Operational Minimums
sub_units.description: Explain warm and cold front behavior, apply mountain-weather cautions, and use ceiling and visibility information to comply with Part 107 minimums and make safe flight decisions.
sub_units.text_content: This section covers frontal weather, mountain flying cautions, and Part 107 ceiling and visibility minimums. Fronts are boundaries between unlike air masses where temperature, humidity, pressure trend, and wind can change rapidly. Mountain operations need careful preflight weather planning and continuous awareness of lee-side turbulence. Ceiling and visibility reports support the regulatory minimums that keep sUAS clear of clouds and in sight. The lessons below cover fronts, mountain cautions, then operational ceiling and visibility minimums.

sub_units.title: Atmospheric Fronts
sub_units.description: Define frontal zones and compare warm versus cold fronts using movement speed, pressure trends, and likely operational weather impacts.
sub_units.text_content:
A frontal zone is the transition area between unlike air masses where weather variables can change quickly over short distances.

Warm front: warm air advances over cooler air, often with broader and longer-duration weather changes; pressure typically falls as the front approaches and improves after passage.

Cold front: colder, denser air undercuts warmer air and typically advances faster with sharper weather changes. A high dew point with falling barometric pressure can indicate approaching frontal weather and rising convective risk.

sub_units.title: Mountain Flying Cautions
sub_units.description: Apply mountain-flight weather planning by interpreting cloud and wind indicators, including lee-side turbulence, rotor/lenticular cues, and wind variation with elevation.
sub_units.text_content:
Before mountain operations, gather cloud reports, wind direction, wind speed, and stability information, then maintain continuous situational awareness because complete information may not always be available.

Wind can differ substantially between mountaintop level and locations partway up the mountain. Stratiform clouds generally indicate more stable air. Convective clouds on windward slopes indicate instability and increased turbulence potential. Standing lenticular and rotor-cloud indicators suggest strong lee-side turbulence, while windward flow may be relatively smoother.

sub_units.title: Operational Ceiling and Visibility Minimums
sub_units.description: Define ceiling and visibility reporting terms and apply Part 107 cloud-clearance and visibility requirements using METAR/automated observations and forecast briefings.
sub_units.text_content:
Ceiling is the lowest cloud layer reported as broken (5/8 to 7/8 coverage) or overcast (8/8 coverage), or vertical visibility into obscurations such as fog or haze. Ceiling is reported in METAR observations and automated weather stations.

Visibility is the greatest horizontal distance at which prominent objects can be seen with the naked eye (unaided vision). Current visibility comes from METARs and automated weather systems; meteorologists also provide predicted visibility in official weather briefings.

Part 107 weather minimums for sUAS operations include at least 3 statute miles (3 SM) visibility and cloud clearance of at least 500 feet below the clouds and 2,000 feet horizontally from clouds. Stay 500 feet below the clouds whenever ceiling is a factor in the flight area.

units.title: LOADING AND PERFORMANCE
units.description: Explain the four forces of flight, weight and balance responsibilities of the RPIC, center of gravity, stability, and how load factor in turns affects stall speed and structural stress.
units.text_content: This unit covers weight, balance, and loading of small unmanned aircraft, then load factors and their effect on performance, stalls, and structural stress. Lessons are grouped into two sections matching the deck: Weight, Balance, and Loading, then Load Factors and Performance.

sub_units.title: Weight, Balance, and Loading
sub_units.description: Apply RPIC weight and balance responsibilities, center of gravity management, and the relationships between weight, lift, and stability.

sub_units.title: Forces in Flight
sub_units.text_content:
In straight & level flight, four forces always act on an aircraft: Lift, Gravity, Thrust, Drag. These forces affect fixed‑wing aircraft and multirotor differently, but the basic principles are the same for all aircraft.

Forces During a TURN:
When an aircraft turns, lift is split into two components: a vertical component that opposes gravity & a horizontal component that makes the aircraft turn. During the turn, the aircraft also experiences centrifugal force, pulling it outward from the center of the turn. This force combines with gravity, increasing the load factor & stress on the aircraft. Pilots must understand how these increased forces affect aircraft performance & adjust their control inputs accordingly.
sub_units.description: Identify the four forces acting on an aircraft and how lift, gravity, and centrifugal force interact during turns.

sub_units.title: Weight and Balance Responsibilities
sub_units.description: Apply RPIC preflight weight and balance duties, maximum gross takeoff weight limits, and the effects of weight changes during flight.
sub_units.text_content:
Pre-Flight Responsibilities:
- Verify aircraft is correctly loaded.
- Determine weight and balance condition of the aircraft.
- Follow manufacturer/builder restrictions for weight and balance.
- Ensure compliance with limits for flight safety.
- Consider consequences of overweight aircraft in emergencies.

Maximum GROSS Takeoff Weight:
Maximum takeoff weight specified by manufacturer but may not guarantee safe takeoff under all conditions.
Conditions requiring weight reduction (3 H):
- High elevation
- High temperature
- High humidity
Other conditions requiring reduction in weight:
- Runway/launch area length
- Surface type and slope
- Surface wind
- Obstacles present

Weight Changes During Flight:
Fuel burn:
- Aircraft becomes lighter → performance improves.
- May negatively affect balance.
Small UA operations:
- Weight change from expendable items (e.g., jettisonable load).
- As battery power goes down the ability to produce lift could decrease.

sub_units.title: Balance and Center of Gravity
sub_units.description: Explain center of gravity limits and shifts, the CG versus center of pressure relationship, and how designers achieve stability.
sub_units.text_content:
Adverse balance conditions affect flight like excess weight.
Balance is made up of two key components:
- Center of Gravity
- Center of Pressure
Manufacturer sets Center of Gravity (CG) limits.

Balance and Center of Gravity (CG) - RPIC Management:
CG is not fixed; depends on weight distribution.
Position shifts as loads move or are used, ex: fuel.
RPIC must:
- Determine CG shift and its effect.
- Ensure CG remains within allowable limits or relocate or shed weight before flight.
- If adding additional cameras or sensors – need to check proper loading.

Gravity:
Gravity - Pulling force that draws bodies toward Earth’s center.
Aircraft weight acts through the Center of Gravity (CG).
CG - Point where all aircraft weight is focused.
- If supported at CG → aircraft balances in any attitude.
CG Location:
- Determined by aircraft design.
- Designers account for center of pressure (CP) travel.

CG vs. CP Relationship - Stability Concept:
CP - Center of lift, the opposite of CG.
The aerodynamic forces of lift occur at the CP.
An aircraft’s weight is concentrated at the CG.
- CG forward of CP → Nose-down tendency.
- CP forward of CG → Nose-up tendency.
Designers make the rear-most allowable position of the center of gravity (CG) ahead of the center of pressure (CP) for stability.

CG vs. CP Relationship - Aircraft Type:
CP and CG on traditionally designed multi-rotors are in the center of the aircraft.
On fixed-wing aircraft, the CP it is about 1/3 back from the leading edge of the wing.

sub_units.title: Weight, Lift, and Stability
sub_units.description: Relate weight to lift in level flight, climbs, and descents, and distinguish stability, maneuverability, and controllability.
sub_units.text_content:
The weight of an aircraft has a direct relationship to the lift generated by its wings or propellers.
Lift:
- Upward force on wing.
- Acts perpendicular to relative wind and aircraft’s lateral axis.
Lift vs. Weight:
- Level flight: Lift = Weight → Equilibrium
- Lift < Weight → aircraft descends
- Lift > Weight → aircraft climbs

Stability:
Stability – The ability of an aircraft to correct for disturbances and return to or maintain its original flight path. Stability is primarily an aircraft design characteristic.

Stability, Maneuverability & Controllability:
Stability – tendency to return to equilibrium.
Maneuverability - Ability to be manipulated easily & handle stress
- Influenced by: Aircraft weight, inertia, size and location of flight controls, and structural strength.
Controllability:
- Aircraft’s ability to respond to pilot input.
- Concerns flight path and attitude.
- A design characteristic – includes the ability to react to up & downdrafts or horizontal winds.

sub_units.title: Load Factors and Performance
sub_units.description: Explain load factor in Gs, its rapid increase with bank angle, and its effect on stall speed, structural stress, and safe operating limits.

sub_units.title: Load Factor Fundamentals
sub_units.description: Define load factor in Gs, explain how turns create structural stress, and state why load factor matters to pilots.
sub_units.text_content:
Measured in Gs (acceleration of gravity):
- 1 G = force of gravity on a body at rest.
- Indicates force experienced when accelerated.
Load Factor – the maximum load factor (at given bank angle) is a proportion between lift and weight and has a trigonometric relationship.

Load:
When an aircraft goes into a turn it experiences a load factor determined by its lift required & angle of its turn.
Any force that deflects an aircraft from a straight path creates stress on its structure.
Load Factor = Amount of this force.
Example:
- Load factor of 3 → aircraft structure supports 3 times its weight.
- Expressed as 3 Gs, 4 Gs, etc.
- You experience more than 1G on your favorite ride.

Load Factors:
Two critical reasons for pilots:
- Dangerous overload can be imposed on aircraft structures.
- Increased load factor raises stalling speed, making stalls possible even at what one would consider safe speeds.
Aircraft are designed to withstand only a certain amount of overload.

sub_units.title: Load Factor in Turns
sub_units.description: Apply the relationships among bank angle, rate of turn, airspeed, and load factor, including the rapid load increase beyond 45-50 degrees of bank.
sub_units.text_content:
Forces in a coordinated turn at constant altitude, load factor results from:
- Centrifugal force (outward force during turn)
- Weight (gravity pulling downward)

RATE of TURN (ROT) and Airspeed:
For a given bank angle:
- Higher airspeed → slower rate of turn
- This compensates for added centrifugal force, keeping load factor constant.

LOAD Factor vs BANK ANGLE - Rapid Increase:
Load factor increases rapidly beyond a 45°–50° bank, and stall speed increases significantly.
Examples:
- 60° bank → 2 Gs
- 80° bank → 5.76 Gs
Wing must produce lift equal to these load factors to maintain altitude.
This chart is in the testing supplement you will have during the test. See how the load factor increases at a significant rate after a bank has reached 45° or 50°. The wing must produce lift equal to these load factors if altitude is to be maintained. Show example with a paper airplane or your drone.

LOAD Factor vs BANK ANGLE - Calculation Example:
Overview: Provides a specific calculation example illustrating the load increase on a 20 lb Unmanned Aircraft (UA) during a 30-degree banked turn.

If a UA weighs 20 lbs, the approximate weight the UA would be required to support during a 30-degree banked turn while maintaining altitude would be: 20 x 1.154 = 23 lbs.

Extreme BANK Angles:
Overview: Discusses the physical limitations of extreme bank angles, noting that a constant-altitude turn is impossible at 90° and that load factors exceed acrobatic limits above 80°.

At 90° bank, constant-altitude turn is not possible.
Aircraft can bank 90° in a slipping turn if not holding altitude.
At slightly more than 80°, load factor exceeds 6Gs (limit for acrobatic aircraft).

sub_units.title: Stalls and Load Factor
sub_units.description: Explain how angle of attack causes stalls and how stalling speed increases with the square root of load factor.
sub_units.text_content:
Any aircraft can stall at any airspeed within structural limits.
Occurs when: Angle of Attack (AOA) becomes too high and the smooth airflow over the wing breaks up and separates.
Resulting in:
- Abrupt change in flight characteristics
- Sudden loss of lift → stall

Stalling SPEED & LOAD Factor:
Stalling speed increases with load factor—it is proportional to the square root of the load factor.
Ex: An aircraft with a normal unaccelerated stalling speed of 50 knots can be stalled at 100 knots by inducing a load factor of 4Gs.
Load factors are measured in Gs (acceleration of gravity) – If a UAV has 4Gs, the total load on a UAVs structure is 4x its actual weight.

sub_units.title: Weight Limits and Consequences
sub_units.description: State the consequences of exceeding weight and balance limits, performance degradations from excessive weight, and compounding safety factors.
sub_units.text_content:
Weight and balance limits are critical for flight safety.
Exceeding maximum weight can:
- Compromise structural integrity.
- Reduce overall aircraft performance.
Center of gravity (CG) → outside allowable limits → results in:
- Control difficulty
- Possible loss of aircraft stability.
RPIC responsible for reviewing aircraft weight & balance data, especially for drones with payloads.

Weight - Definition:
Weight = force of gravity acting on an object.
Determined by:
- The object’s mass
- Earth’s gravitational acceleration
Weight is constantly acting downward and must be counteracted by lift.

Weight - Lift Dependence:
Amount of lift depends on:
- Airfoil design
- Angle of attack (AOA)
- Airspeed
- Air density
If aircraft weight exceeds available lift → flight may be impossible.

Weight - Excessive Weight Degradations:
Excessive weight negatively impacts many aspects of flight including failing to take off.
Key Performance Degradations:
- Higher takeoff speed required
- Longer takeoff distance
- Reduced rate & angle of climb
- Lower maximum altitude
- Shorter flight range
- Reduced cruising speed
- Reduced maneuverability
- Higher stall speed
- Higher approach & landing speeds
- Longer landing distance

Safety Considerations:
Overloading becomes even more dangerous when combined with:
- High altitude
- High density altitude
- Strong winds
- High temperatures
In emergencies excessive weight can reduce the pilot’s ability to respond effectively.

sub_units.title: Key Takeaways
sub_units.description: Summarize load factor, its measurement in Gs, and its effect on stall speed and structural stress.
sub_units.text_content:
Load factor = stress on aircraft structure during turn.
Measured in Gs (gravity units).
Higher load factor → higher stall speed and greater structural stress.
Bank angle increases load factor significantly.

units.title: EMERGENCY PROCEDURES
units.description: Prepare for and handle unexpected in-flight emergencies, covering RPIC planning responsibilities, crew briefing, regulatory deviation authority, and post-emergency documentation.
units.text_content:
Overview: This unit outlines how to prepare for and handle unexpected in-flight emergencies, covering the Remote Pilot in Command's (RPIC) responsibilities for planning, crew briefing, regulatory deviation authority, and required post-emergency documentation.

Introduction to Emergency Procedures
An in‑flight emergency is an unexpected event that can create serious risks for an unprepared remote pilot. The RPIC is responsible for safe operation of the Unmanned Aircraft (UA) at all times & should plan for emergencies in the preflight planning process.

sub_units.title: Emergency Preparedness and Response
sub_units.text_content:
Potential Hazards and Accident Causes:
Some examples of unexpected events that could cause accidents are:
- Unexpected Manned Aircraft Entering the Area
- Propeller or Motor Malfunction
- Wildlife Interference
- Battery Depletion Faster Than Expected
- Unexpected Obstacles

Preflight Planning, Checklists, and Crew Briefing:
Preparation and Crew Management
- Checklists: Some manufacturers provide preflight checklists for safe operations. If no manufacturer checklist exists, the remote pilot must create one to ensure safety.
- Crew Briefing: All crew members must be briefed on operational details and emergency procedures. Having an emergency plan that everyone has been briefed on enables the crew to remain calm, as training will kick in. When additional crew members are used, they must all be briefed before the flight.

Regulatory Deviation and Documentation:
Overview: Explaining the remote pilot's authority to break Part 107 rules for safety during an emergency and the requirements for post-emergency action and reporting.

Authority to Deviate
- Deviation: During an emergency, a remote pilot may deviate from any Part 107 regulation if necessary for safety.
- Return to Normal: Once the emergency has ended, the remote pilot must return to normal Part 107 operating regulations.
- Documentation: Document what happened once you return to safety, including videos or pictures.
- Reporting: When rules are broken for safety, reporting to the FAA is only required when asked.

Example Emergency Scenario:
Example: Manned Aircraft Hazard
- Scenario: Creating a video at a beach; weather is clear and the area is low-risk. You complete preflight tasks, establish your takeoff/landing zone, and brief your Visual Observer (VO).
- Hazard Detected (Before Launch): You notice a helicopter flying low where you were planning to fly.
- Required Action: Since you haven’t launched, keep the UA grounded, maintain visuals of the helicopter, communicate with the crew, reassess the situation after the aircraft passes, update your risk assessment before flying, and launch when completely clear.
- Action (If Airborne): If you were already airborne, you would make decisions to avoid causing an in‑flight emergency.
sub_units.description: Identify common in-flight emergency causes, apply preflight checklist and crew briefing requirements, explain the RPIC’s authority to deviate from Part 107 in an emergency, and walk through an example emergency scenario.

units.title: AERONAUTICAL DECISION MAKING
units.description: By the end of this unit, you will explain Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) and apply risk management, hazardous attitude antidotes, CRM/SRM, physiology and vision factors, and maintenance responsibilities to safer sUAS operations.
units.text_content: Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) gives remote pilots a systematic way to choose the safest course of action using current information. This unit applies ADM to risk management, hazardous attitudes, crew and single-pilot resource management, pilot fitness and vision, and aircraft maintenance.

sub_units.title: Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
sub_units.text_content: ADM is a systematic process pilots use to choose the best course of action for a specific situation. It supports consistent, informed decisions as conditions change. Because human error is a leading cause of aviation accidents, ADM is essential to safe flight operations.
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will explain what ADM is, why it is systematic, and why it is critical to reducing human error in aviation.

sub_units.title: Steps to Good Decision Making
sub_units.text_content:
1. Identify personal attitudes hazardous to safe flight.
  2. Learn behavior-modification techniques—replace hazardous attitudes with safer, more accurate thinking.
  3. Learn how to recognize and deal with stress.
  4. Develop risk-assessment skills—evaluate hazards with tools such as PAVE, CARE, and DECIDE.
    • CARE: Consider consequences, Alternatives, Reality, and External pressures before choosing an action.
    • DECIDE: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, and Evaluate.
  5. Use all available resources.
  6. Evaluate the effectiveness of your ADM skills—does the outcome support safety and mission goals?
sub_units.description: Apply all six ADM decision-making steps: identify hazardous attitudes, modify behavior, manage stress, assess risk, use available resources, and evaluate the outcome.

sub_units.title: Risk Management
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will describe risk management goals, decision foundations and principles, and continuous before/during/after flight risk review including AAR.

sub_units.title: Hazards and Risk Assessment
sub_units.text_content:
A hazard is a real or perceived condition, event, or circumstance that a pilot encounters. Different pilots may assess the same hazard differently, so the pilot assigns a value to its potential impact, determines the degree of risk, and chooses the best way to mitigate it. This assessment continues throughout the flight. Severity Levels (Event Occurrence Likelihood)
  • Probable: The event will occur several times.
  • Occasional: The event will probably occur sometime.
  • Remote: The event is unlikely to occur, but possible.
  • Improbable: The event is highly unlikely to occur.
sub_units.description: Define a hazard and risk, detailing the pilot's role in assessing risk severity, and listing the four levels of event occurrence likelihood.

sub_units.title: Hazardous Attitudes and Antidotes
sub_units.text_content:
Hazardous attitudes can negatively affect pilot judgment, putting everyone at risk, but can be countered by redirecting those attitudes toward safer, more appropriate actions.
Recognition of hazardous thoughts is the first step toward defusing them.
After recognizing it as hazardous, the pilot should label it as hazardous, then state the corresponding antidote.
Pilots should memorize the antidotes for each hazardous attitude for the test.
Common hazardous attitudes and antidotes:
- Anti-authority (“Don’t tell me”) -> Follow the rules; they are usually right.
- Impulsivity (“Do something quickly”) -> Not so fast; think first.
- Invulnerability (“It won’t happen to me”) -> It could happen to me.
- Macho (“I can do it”) -> Taking chances is foolish.
- Resignation (“What’s the use”) -> I can make a difference.
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will recognize hazardous attitudes and apply the corresponding antidote mindset to support safer decisions.

sub_units.title: Mitigating Risks: IMSAFE and PAVE Checklists
sub_units.text_content: IMSAFE Checklist The IMSAFE checklist helps determine whether everyone on the team is physically and mentally ready for the operation. If a team member is not well, the crew, equipment, and public are put at risk. Because operators self-certify their fitness, failure to assess readiness can lead to fatigue, unclear thinking, and poor decisions when problems arise. PAVE Checklist PAVE helps pilots identify and manage risk before flight. It organizes hazards into four areas: Pilot, Aircraft, Environment, and External Pressures (including life and work pressures). The RPIC decides whether it is safe to fly, identifies the risks, and determines whether they can be managed successfully. If the flight proceeds, the RPIC develops mitigations such as personal minimums and checklists while maintaining situational awareness.
sub_units.description: Use IMSAFE to assess crew fitness and PAVE to identify operational hazards and support preflight go/no-go decisions.

sub_units.text_content:
Goal Identify safety-related hazards before they happen and mitigate or remove the risks. Foundation of Decisions Decisions are based on a combination of:
  • Direct experience: e.g., a driver gets hurt from not wearing a seat belt.
  • Indirect experience: e.g., seeing someone else injured from not wearing a seat belt.
  • Education and training: RPICs develop experience not only through their own flights, but by studying accidents, reports, and lessons learned from others.
Principles of Risk Management
  • Accept Unnecessary Risk—Is the outcome worth the risk?
  • Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level—usually, the RPIC.
  • Integrate Risk Management Into All Phases of Flight—an ongoing process, not a one-time step.
  • Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs.
Process Use an ongoing cycle in which participants constantly reassess risks and determine whether their controls are reducing those risks. Application Use risk management throughout the operation—before, during, and after flight. Post-Flight Conduct an After Action Review (AAR) after each job to discuss what went right, what went wrong, and what can be learned for the next operation.

sub_units.title: Workload and Crew Resource Management
sub_units.description: Apply workload management, Crew Resource Management (CRM), and Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM) to communication, leadership, decision making, situational awareness, and safe operations.

sub_units.title: Effective Team Communication
sub_units.text_content:
Before launch, the RPIC chooses how the crew will communicate and confirms a backup method. During flight, short, clear reports keep everyone aware of hazards and changes. Remember
  • Use radios, phones, or headsets to relay information and manage tasks.
  • Have a backup communication method.
  • Use the phonetic alphabet to reduce misunderstandings.
  • The RPIC establishes the communication plan and announces changes.
  • The Visual Observer reports hazards while maintaining visual contact with the aircraft.
  • Keep every crewmember in the loop.
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will explain crew communication methods, backup communication planning, and RPIC/VO communication responsibilities.

sub_units.title: Workload Management
sub_units.text_content:
Workload management means planning people and resources, then prioritizing the tasks that matter most without overloading anyone. An overloaded crewmember may miss a hazard or make a poor decision. Remember
  • Prioritize safety-critical tasks.
  • Assign clear responsibilities.
  • Do not give a crewmember more work than they can safely manage.
  • Use radios, weather applications, and other technology to collect and share information.
  • Work smarter, not harder.
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will apply workload management principles to prioritize tasks, avoid overload, and use technology to support safer decisions.

sub_units.title: Situational Awareness
sub_units.text_content:
Situational awareness means knowing what is happening now and anticipating what may happen next. A pilot must keep the entire operation in view instead of fixating on one task. Monitor the whole situation
  • Pilot: Fitness, workload, and readiness.
  • Aircraft: Position, condition, battery, and performance.
  • Environment: Weather, terrain, obstacles, people, and other aircraft.
  • Operation: Mission status, crew actions, and changing risks.
Common threats
  • Fatigue, stress, and excessive workload can cause fixation and make the pilot ignore other hazards.
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will define situational awareness, identify its key elements, and recognize common threats that degrade it.

sub_units.text_content:
A safe operation depends on how well people use the resources around them. With a crew, the RPIC coordinates people and information; when operating alone, the pilot must deliberately perform those same checks without a second person to catch mistakes. Crew Resource Management (CRM) CRM is the effective use of all available resources. Remember the four resource groups:
  • People: RPIC, visual observers, other crew, and outside support.
  • Equipment: Aircraft, controller, batteries, radios, and safety equipment.
  • Technical resources: Checklists, procedures, applications, charts, and weather tools.
  • Information: Weather, airspace, aircraft status, hazards, and crew reports.
CRM focuses on
  • Communication.
  • Leadership.
  • Decision making.
  • Situational awareness.
  • Teamwork.
A formal procedure or Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) helps the crew apply CRM consistently and reduce operational risk. Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM) SRM is the process a pilot uses to gather information, understand the situation, and make a safe decision when operating alone. Remember to:
  • Gather information before and during flight.
  • Recognize the problem and study the situation.
  • Choose, perform, and reassess the safest action.
  • Use personal experience, skill level, and personal minimums.
  • Check physical condition and mental readiness before deciding.
  • Double-check critical items because no second crewmember is present.
SRM requires judgment, not just technique—THINK.

sub_units.title: Physiology
sub_units.description: Identify physiological conditions and vision limitations that affect pilot performance, then apply readiness, scanning, and collision-threat practices to safer sUAS operations.

sub_units.title: Physiology
sub_units.description: Recognize physiological and environmental conditions that can impair a crewmember and apply the Part 107 requirement that every participant be able to perform duties safely.
sub_units.text_content:
A remote pilot may begin a job feeling capable, then become impaired by heat, dehydration, fatigue, stress, medication, or breathing problems. The RPIC must continually assess the crew—not only at launch—because Part 107 prohibits an operation when the RPIC, person manipulating the controls, or Visual Observer cannot perform their duties safely. Conditions to remember
  • Hypoxia: Reduced oxygen.
  • Hyperventilation: May cause visual impairment, temperature or tingling sensations, dizziness, lightheadedness, or unconsciousness.
  • Stress and fatigue: Reduce attention, judgment, and reaction time.
  • Dehydration: Can impair physical and mental performance.
  • Heatstroke, sunburn, and frostbite: Dress appropriately and use shelter when needed.
  • Alcohol and drugs: Prescription and over-the-counter medications, including some antihistamines and decongestants, may cause drowsiness or other impairment.

sub_units.title: Vision
sub_units.text_content:
A small aircraft can disappear against terrain or sky, and another aircraft may not appear threatening until its motion becomes clear. Effective vision technique combines a deliberate scan with peripheral awareness. Scanning technique
  1. Scan from right to left or left to right.
  2. Begin at the greatest distance where an object can be perceived, then move inward.
  3. Pause at viewing points covering approximately 30°.
  4. Stop for 2–3 seconds depending on the detail required.
  5. Overlap the previous field of view by about 10° when moving to the next point.
Vision and threat cues
  • Peripheral vision is especially useful for detecting movement.
  • If visual contact with the sUA is lost, make small viewing movements left or right or direct a Visual Observer to scan specific sectors.
  • Movement is often the first indication of a collision threat.
  • An aircraft with no apparent relative motion is likely on a collision course—take immediate evasive action.
sub_units.description: Apply see-and-avoid scanning techniques, recover visual contact with the sUA, and recognize collision-threat cues that require immediate evasive action.

sub_units.text_content: The remote pilot is part of the flight system. Physical condition can weaken judgment and reaction time, while vision limitations can hide traffic or cause the pilot to lose sight of the aircraft. The two lessons below separate physiological readiness from vision, scanning, and collision-threat detection.

sub_units.title: Maintenance and Inspection Procedures
sub_units.description: By the end of this lesson, you will apply Part 107 maintenance and inspection requirements, including manufacturer guidance, self-developed programs, documentation, and RPIC accountability.
sub_units.text_content:
Part 107 Requirements Part 107 requires all sUAS operators to ensure their aircraft is safe for operation. Maintenance includes scheduled and unscheduled maintenance, repair, inspection, modification, replacement, and system software upgrades for the sUAS and its components. Follow manufacturer instructions and recommendations. The RPIC must verify the aircraft is safe before flight even when someone else performed the maintenance; some manufacturers require certified repair personnel. Self-Developed Program FAA guidance in AC 107-2A says that when the manufacturer does not provide a maintenance program, the operator should create one covering:
  • Scheduled inspections.
  • Replacement intervals for propellers, motors, batteries, and other components.
  • System and firmware updates.
  • Cleaning procedures.
  • Records of all maintenance performed.
Qualified personnel should perform maintenance, and all work should be documented. The RPIC remains responsible for verifying that work completed by other team members was done correctly before flight.

units.title: RADIO COMMUNICATION PROCEDURES
units.description: Interpret radio communication in the National Airspace System, find and understand airport advisory frequencies, and recognize aircraft identification and standard inbound calls—without transmitting unless it is an emergency.
units.text_content: Remote pilots normally listen rather than transmit. Understanding radio phraseology, frequencies, call signs, and inbound announcements helps the RPIC anticipate manned-aircraft activity near an operation. Do NOT transmit on aviation frequencies unless it is an emergency.

sub_units.title: Radio Communication Fundamentals
sub_units.description: Explain why radio communication matters in the NAS, recognize standard phraseology, and use the ICAO phonetic alphabet to interpret aircraft communications.
sub_units.text_content:
Radio communication helps pilots share information before, during, and after flight, including unexpected weather and in-flight emergencies. Remote pilots use that information to understand nearby manned-aircraft activity. Proper radio procedures
  • Use standard terminology from the AIM Pilot/Controller Glossary.
  • Use the phonetic alphabet for aircraft identification; do not invent substitute words.
  • Listen for clear, concise reports about position, intentions, weather, and emergencies.
  • Monitoring a local tower frequency may be required by an airspace authorization.
ICAO phonetic alphabet Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, Golf, Hotel, India, Juliet, Kilo, Lima, Mike, November, Oscar, Papa, Quebec, Romeo, Sierra, Tango, Uniform, Victor, Whiskey, X-ray, Yankee, Zulu.

sub_units.title: CTAF, Frequencies, and Advisory Services
sub_units.description: Use Chart Supplements and sectional charts to find CTAF information, then distinguish UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS, and closed-tower advisory frequencies near non-towered airports.
sub_units.text_content:
Before operating near a non-towered airport, check the Chart Supplement and sectional chart for the correct frequency and remain alert for traffic. CTAF is the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency used for airport advisory communications. It may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, Flight Service Station (FSS), or tower frequency when the tower is closed. Remote pilots should understand the traffic and phraseology they hear, but should not transmit unless it is an emergency. UNICOM—commonly 122.8 UNICOM is a non-government station at an airport without an operating control tower or FSS. When available, it may provide:
  • Runway in use.
  • Local weather observations.
  • Airport conditions.
UNICOM advisories are not ATC instructions; pilots still self-announce and maintain traffic awareness. MULTICOM—122.9 At a non-towered airport with no UNICOM or other listed frequency, pilots use MULTICOM as the CTAF to self-announce their position and intentions. Flight Service Station (FSS) FSS provides preflight and in-flight services, including:
  • Weather briefings.
  • Flight-plan processing.
  • Search-and-rescue initiation.
  • NOTAM updates.
Unlike ATC, FSS does not issue clearances.

sub_units.title: Aircraft Identification and Standard Radio Calls
sub_units.description: Interpret aircraft registration and operator call signs, then recognize the standard format of an initial 10-mile inbound call at a non-towered airport.
sub_units.text_content:
Call signs tell listeners who is transmitting, while the location and intention in a radio call tell them what that aircraft is about to do. U.S. registrations begin with “N” and are spoken with the phonetic alphabet. Aircraft identification
  • Light general aviation: Manufacturer name plus registration; e.g., “Cessna One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo.”
  • Turboprop or jet: Model name plus registration; e.g., “Citation One-Two-Three-Alpha-Bravo.”
  • Airline: Company call sign plus flight number; e.g., “Southwest Seven-One-One.”
  • Some airlines use special call signs; British Airways uses “Speedbird.”
Initial 10-mile inbound call A common call states the airport, aircraft identification, distance and direction, intention, and airport again: “Town and Country traffic, Cessna One-Two-Three Bravo Foxtrot is 10 miles south inbound for landing, Town and Country traffic.”
